contributions.text_english: We will move immediately now to item 1, questions to the First Minister. Question 1, Alun Cox.
contributions.text_original: Symudwn nawr yn syth at eitem 1, cwestiynau i'r Prif Weinidog. Cwestiwn 1, Alun Cox.

contributions.text_english: 1. What assessment has the Government made of whether current school transport arrangements meet the needs of pupils with additional learning needs in Afan Ogwr Rhondda? OQ64716
contributions.text_original: 1. Pa asesiad mae'r Llywodraeth wedi'i wneud i ganfod a yw'r trefniadau cludiant ysgol presennol yn diwallu anghenion disgyblion ag anghenion dysgu ychwanegol yn Afan Ogwr Rhondda? OQ64716

contributions.text_english: Good afternoon. Whilst it's for the local authorities in Afan Ogwr Rhondda to assess the school transport needs of all pupils, we as a Government are of course keen to see effective provision that meets everyone’s needs. This is of even greater importance for pupils with additional learning needs, because transport can be a real barrier to them accessing the education that they need.
contributions.text_original: Prynhawn da. Er mai cyfrifoldeb yr awdurdodau lleol yn Afan Ogwr Rhondda ydy asesu anghenion cludiant disgyblion i’r ysgol, mi ydyn ni fel Llywodraeth wrth gwrs yn awyddus i weld darpariaeth effeithiol sy’n diwallu anghenion pawb. Mae hyn yn bwysicach fyth i ddisgyblion efo anghenion dysgu ychwanegol, gan fod cludiant yn gallu bod yn rhwystr gwirioneddol iddyn nhw allu cael mynediad at yr addysg y maen nhw ei hangen.

contributions.text_english: Thank you, First Minister. Rhondda Cynon Taf council has retained discretionary school transport for some of its most vulnerable learners, including those with additional learning needs. At the same time, the general cost of transport from home to school in Rhondda Cynon Taf has increased significantly, from £10.5 million in 2021-22 to £16.9 million according to forecasts for 2025-26. We know that some learners with additional learning needs have more complex transport needs than others and that suitable transport arrangements can be vital to ensure that they can access their education. Can the First Minister explain how the Welsh Government is working with local authorities to ensure that they receive the funding that they need to continue to meet the different transport needs of pupils with additional learning needs?
contributions.text_original: Diolch, Brif Weinidog. Mae cyngor Rhondda Cynon Taf wedi cadw cludiant ysgol tybiedig ar gyfer rhai o'r dysgwyr mwyaf agored i niwed, gan gynnwys y rheini ag anghenion dysgu ychwanegol. Ar yr un pryd, mae cost gyffredinol cludiant o'r cartref i'r ysgol yn Rhondda Cynon Taf yn cynyddu yn sylweddol, o £10.5 miliwn yn 2021-22 i £16.9 miliwn yn y rhagolygon ar gyfer 2025-26. Gwyddom fod gan rai dysgwyr ag anghenion dysgu ychwanegol anghenion cludiant mwy cymhleth nag eraill ac y gall cludiant priodol fod yn hanfodol i sicrhau eu bod yn gallu mynd i’w haddysg. A all y Prif Weinidog esbonio sut mae Llywodraeth Cymru yn cydweithio ag awdurdodau lleol i sicrhau eu bod yn cael y cyllid sydd ei angen i barhau i ateb anghenion cludiant gwahanol disgyblion ag anghenion dysgu ychwanegol?

contributions.text_english:
I welcome the decision made by Rhondda Cynon Taf to retain its discretionary transport provision for some of the most vulnerable learners. We certainly recognise that transport to school for pupils with ALN can often be much more complex, as it can perhaps require specialist vehicles or assistance from others. And in that context, of course, decisions must take into account the long-term sustainability, whilst retaining that focus on the results that we need to see now, ensuring that pupils, above all else, can access education, and can do that regularly and take a full part in school life. 

Additional learning needs and transport were discussed with leaders of local authorities in September, along with the Welsh Local Government Association. And we are continuing to work closely with the WLGA to strengthen learner travel provision and also to respond to changes in patterns across Wales.
contributions.text_original:
Dwi'n croesawu penderfyniad Rhondda Cynon Taf i gario ymlaen efo darpariaeth trafnidiaeth dewisol—discretionary, felly—ar gyfer rhai o’r dysgwyr mwyaf bregus. Rydyn ni’n sicr yn cydnabod bod trafnidiaeth i ddysgwyr efo anghenion dysgu ychwanegol yn gallu bod yn fwy cymhleth yn aml iawn, yn golygu’r angen am gerbydau arbenigol o bosib neu gynhorthwy gan eraill. Ac mae’n rhaid, wrth gwrs, yn y cyd-destun hwnnw, i benderfyniadau ystyried cynaliadwyedd hirdymor, tra'n cadw’r ffocws yna ar y canlyniadau rydyn ni angen eu gweld rŵan, yn sicrhau bod dysgwyr, uwchlaw popeth, yn gallu cael mynediad at addysg, ac yn gallu gwneud hynny yn rheolaidd a chymryd rhan yn llawn mewn bywyd ysgol.

Mi gafodd anghenion dysgu ychwanegol a thrafnidiaeth ei drafod efo arweinyddion llywodraeth leol ym mis Medi, efo’r WLGA. Mi rydyn ni'n parhau i weithio’n agos efo’r WLGA i gryfhau teithio i ddysgwyr ac i ymateb hefyd i newidiadau mewn patrymau ledled Cymru.

contributions.text_english: Parents across Afan Ogwr Rhondda are deeply concerned about their children's school transport arrangements. A survey conducted, with 176 respondents from Rhondda Cynon Taf, found that 72 respondents reported attendance disruption for their children due to insufficient school transport arrangements. A hundred and twenty-five people described feeling anxiety, vulnerability, stress or fear as a result. Reliability, capacity and safety are seriously important, especially when a child faces additional barriers to their learning. So, when assessments are made on transport provision, what will your Government do to ensure that vulnerable learners are not left behind by decisions that are driven by costs rather than outcomes?

contributions.text_english: As I said earlier, this is very much a live issue, making sure that, when it comes to additional learning needs learners in particular, those particular circumstances that are relevant to them are taken into account. Funding for school transport, remember, comes through the revenue support grant. It is for local authorities to make provision, but the rise in school transport costs is a complex issue. It is driven by a number of factors. And whether that's local government or the Welsh Government, and the way we interact with this, addressing those complexities requires action across portfolios at local and national level. We, as I say, have been discussing with the WLGA those kinds of pressures that we realise are on local government, at the same time as making the case to the UK Government on the issues that they can take decisions to address—on fuel costs, for example. So, this is something that needs to be addressed on many, many levels.

contributions.text_english: 2. What action is the Government taking to support the creation of community energy projects and ensure that the benefits of Wales’s natural resources are retained in Wales? OQ64708
contributions.text_original: 2. Pa gamau mae'r Llywodraeth yn eu cymryd i gefnogi'r gwaith o greu prosiectau ynni cymunedol a sicrhau bod manteision adnoddau naturiol Cymru yn cael eu cadw yng Nghymru? OQ64708

contributions.text_english: Welsh Government investment through Ynni Cymru is generating real savings and benefits for the community. I was delighted just a few weeks ago to visit the Iqra Masjid mosque in Newport to see one project first-hand for myself. Our plans to establish a new Welsh public energy company will support our ambition in the national energy strategy for more of the energy generated in Wales to be owned in Wales and to benefit Wales. More Welsh ownership will see the value created from our natural resources retained for the people of Wales, which is something I hope all of us would want to pursue.

More Welsh ownership will see the value created from our natural resources retained for the people of Wales, which is something I hope all of us would want to pursue.

contributions.text_english: First Minister, I'm proud to support a grass-roots campaign in Pen-y-bont Bro Morgannwg to stop the proposed small modular reactor nuclear project in the Llynfi valley by Last Energy. More extractive and harmful projects are not what our post-industrial communities deserve. It's no surprise why they have selected one of our most deprived communities to pilot this new nuclear technology. Campaigners across the constituency are calling out for renewable energy projects that they can directly benefit from, and that's why we're exploring alternative energy options within the constituency rather than accepting private organisations coming in to extract the profits from our communities. So, Prif Weinidog, will you reaffirm this Government's ambition to ensure that our communities benefit from energy projects?

Campaigners across the constituency are calling out for renewable energy projects that they can directly benefit from, and that's why we're exploring alternative energy options within the constituency rather than accepting private organisations coming in to extract the profits from our communities. So, Prif Weinidog, will you reaffirm this Government's ambition to ensure that our communities benefit from energy projects?

contributions.text_english: Yes, absolutely. In many ways, that principle is agnostic of that source of power generation. Energy projects in Wales must show, I think, how they improve matters for people in Wales. It's an important issue that will be at the heart of the national energy strategy we have committed to delivering. Through that strategy, we will deliver that commitment to make sure that Welsh people and communities have more ownership, as I say, of energy initiatives, and that they and their communities receive also their fair share of the profits. We need a balanced energy system that delivers secure supply. Renewables will be an important part of that system, obviously. The public energy company that we're currently consulting on will have a vital role, I think, to play in supporting communities and securing value from commercially led projects too.

contributions.text_english: First Minister, Wales presently has nearly 4,000 MW of installed capacity, all dependent on gas for firing. Given what's just been said, this document, produced by the National Grid, 'Community Energy Scenarios', reveals the truth of this community energy nonsense. At best—at best—it will mean we go from 47 MW to 281 MW by 2035. To be fair to you, you're not a Nimby First Minister, but what I would describe Plaid's nuclear policy as is 'only in Rhun's back yard', because that's effectively what we've got. First Minister, right across south Wales, we have a growing energy problem. Will you reconsider Plaid's energy policy so that we can look at a series of small modular reactors right across south Wales?

contributions.text_english: Will we reconsider our energy strategy? I think I've confirmed again today that we are bringing forward a new national energy strategy that calls for that balanced energy system. Referring to community energy 'nonsense'—talk to people in Bethesda about the 'nonsense' that is their energy production scheme, which they are hugely proud of and that brings all sorts of benefits to that community. Look at all those projects across Wales, including the one I visited in Newport recently, that people take a real, genuine sense of ownership of and know that they are tackling the energy crisis that we are facing, plus the climate change crisis that his party is denying. Our energy future will bring together all sorts of technologies, all sorts of production methods. I want to use our resources for the benefit of the people of Wales, but at the heart of that has to be something that is very different to the extractive story of the past and that has the interests of Wales at the very heart of it—something that Reform really struggle with.

contributions.text_english: Community energy schemes, like larger schemes, also require access to the grid. I want to see sustainable schemes and the grid infrastructure being delivered across Wales in order to deliver the benefits that we want to see for our local communities.

contributions.text_english: First Minister, what steps are you taking, working with the UK Government, Ofgem and network operators, to ensure that connection costs and waiting times don't prevent these projects, be they community or larger scale, from progressing? We need that grid infrastructure in place for it to succeed. I think Wales has got an opportunity to be an energy superpower, and that's why the comments from the Plaid Cymru Member earlier about SMRs are so disappointing. So, can you, further to my first question, explain why SMRs are the right solution for Anglesey but not for south Wales?

contributions.text_english:
To answer that question, this is a developing technology, and it makes sense to develop it on a site where past nuclear skills exist. But the question is broader than that, of course. I don't think that there's a great deal of disagreement between us, truth be told, on the need to make the most of our natural resources as a nation, to ensure that we can produce more energy using our natural resources, be that wind, wave, tide or whatever.

I agree also on the need to ensure that the system that we have to distribute that electricity should be resilient for the future. We're going to need a lot more electricity in the future, and that electricity has to get to our communities and leave the sites of production. But, once again, I return to this central point that that can be done in collaboration with our communities, ensuring that there is no exploitation. I also agree with the fact that that has to happen in collaboration with the UK Government, and so on. So, there is an agenda here. I hope we can build consensus on it. There will be difficult decisions in relation to that agenda, but we are building an independent energy future for ourselves as a nation, along with all the benefits that will flow from that.
contributions.text_original:
I ateb y cwestiwn yna, mae hwn yn dechnoleg sydd yn datblygu, ac mae o'n gwneud synnwyr i'w ddatblygu ar safle lle mae yna sgiliau niwclear o'r gorffennol. Ond mae'r cwestiwn yn ehangach na hynny, wrth gwrs. Dwi ddim yn meddwl bod yna lawer o anghytuno rhyngom ni, mewn difri, ar yr angen i wneud yn fawr o'n hadnoddau naturiol ni fel gwlad, i sicrhau ein bod ni'n gallu cynhyrchu mwy o ynni yn defnyddio'n adnoddau naturiol ni, pa un ai yn wynt neu'n donnau neu'n llanw, neu beth bynnag.

Dwi'n cytuno hefyd ar yr angen i sicrhau bod y system sydd gennym ni i drosglwyddo a dosbarthu'r trydan yna yn wydn ar gyfer y dyfodol. Rydyn ni'n mynd i fod angen llawer mwy o drydan yn y dyfodol, ac mae'n rhaid i'r trydan yna gyrraedd ein cymunedau ni a gadael y llefydd lle mae'n cael ei gynhyrchu. Ond, unwaith eto, dwi'n dod yn ôl at y pwynt canolog yma fod modd gwneud hynny mewn cydweithrediad efo ein cymunedau ni, yn gwneud yn siŵr nad oes yna ecsbloetio. Hefyd, dwi'n cytuno ar y ffaith bod hynny'n gorfod digwydd mewn cydweithrediad efo Llywodraeth y Deyrnas Unedig, ac yn y blaen. Felly, mae yna agenda yn fan hyn. Dwi'n gobeithio y gallwn ni adeiladu consensws drosto fo. Mae yna benderfyniadau anodd ynghlwm wrtho, ond adeiladu dyfodol ynni annibynnol ar gyfer ein hunain fel gwlad yr ydym ni a'r holl fuddiannau a fydd yn llifo o hynny.

contributions.text_english: I now call the party leaders to question the First Minister. First of all, the leader of Reform UK, Helen Jenner.
contributions.text_original: Galwaf yn awr ar arweinwyr y pleidiau i holi'r Prif Weinidog. Yn gyntaf, arweinydd Reform UK, Helen Jenner.

contributions.text_english: Diolch, Lywydd. First Minister, I want to raise a deeply disturbing case from our capital city. In March this year, 29-year-old Mohammed Abbas arrived in Britain on a small boat from France. By June, he was in custody facing criminal charges. In July, he was convicted of offences including assaulting a police officer and sentenced to 300 hours of community service. He was subsequently placed in Home Office-funded accommodation in Cardiff. Just two days later, at 2 o'clock in the morning, he entered a family home and committed sexual offences in the presence of two young girls, both under the age of 16. He has since pleaded guilty to four further offences and is awaiting sentencing. Those two young girls should have been safe in their own home. First Minister, what discussions have you had with the Home Office about this case? What assurances have you sought about the safeguarding of communities hosting asylum accommodation? And will you now commission an urgent review of the arrangements between Welsh public services and the Home Office to ensure that a case like this is never repeated?

contributions.text_english:
I think I would refer the Member to the safeguarding work that this Government is doing in general, making sure that we are strengthening the provisions that we put in place as a Welsh Government to safeguard the citizens of Wales. What has been described to me—and it's not a case that I am familiar with myself—is criminality. What has been described to me are the actions of an individual that all of us would condemn and that the legal system should be empowered to deal with.

I know that it is always the case that Reform seeks only to comment on those elements of criminality that emerge from people who have come into the UK, but that really doesn't help us when it comes to the core issue here, which is to make sure that we in Wales, in the public sector, in the Welsh Government, have safeguarding measures in place across the board that make sure that we de-risk and that we look after those vulnerable people within our society.

First Minister, last week your Deputy Minister for Transport announced yet another 18-month study into congestion on the M4 around Newport, alongside proposals that could see motorway junctions closed. Let's not forget it was the Labour Government who scrapped the relief road, wasting well over £100 million of taxpayers' money in the process. Closing motorway junctions doesn't make the traffic disappear; it simply moves the problem elsewhere, and restricts emergency services trying to carry out their duties. First Minister, Newport needs a long-term solution that improves capacity, not measures that redistribute congestion into residential communities. So, I'll ask you a straightforward question and I expect a straightforward answer: does your Government intend to press ahead with building an M4 relief road around Newport during this Senedd term—yes or no?

Inaction, we have decided, is not an option for this new Plaid Cymru Government. contributions.text_english: Well, it's a 'no', and it's a shame to see that you're determined to continue Mark Drakeford's war on motorists. Nothing changes, does it? The cosy Cardiff consensus continues. Speaking of which, First Minister, throughout the Senedd election, you promised Wales you would deliver change, but we've learned this morning that you've done a deal with Labour to push through your failed supplementary budget. When Labour were in power, it was your party that was propping them up, voting through their budgets as they destroyed our public services. Now you're in power, it's Labour who are nodding along as your Government sends millions of pounds abroad while our NHS suffers. When you said you'd deliver change, people expected you to change more than just the seating plan in the Chamber. And I know a few things about seating plans. So, First Minister, how much longer will the people of Wales have to wait for a Government prepared to deliver real change?

The seating plan on that side of the Chamber seems to be changing every week. [Laughter.] And I would suggest that maybe she doesn't make herself too comfortable where she is either.

contributions.text_english: Leader of the Welsh Conservatives, Darren Millar.
contributions.text_original: Arweinydd y Ceidwadwyr Cymreig, Darren Millar.

contributions.text_english:
Diolch, Lywydd. Look, Labour didn't fold, they collapsed. Isn't that the case?

First Minister, people across Wales are facing a cost-of-living crisis, yet senior managers in the public sector and in publicly funded organisations are enjoying pay packets that people in our country could only dream of. And what's really galling is that the worse their organisations seem to perform, the better the pay packet seems to be.

Let's take Transport for Wales, for example. Last year, it was one of the worst performing rail companies across the whole of the United Kingdom in terms of cancellations, yet its chief executive is earning nearly £0.25 million every single year. Then there's Cardiff Airport. It currently receives £20 million per year in annual subsidy from the Welsh Government just to stay afloat, yet its latest financial statements show that its highest paid director received a package of more than £275,000 per year. And in north Wales, Betsi Cadwaladr University Health Board has the worst performing emergency departments and longest waiting times in the country, yet its chief executive is earning a salary of £262,500 per year. It's scandalous. 

So, do you agree with me, First Minister, that these salaries are now completely out of control, they bear no relationship to the performance of their organisations, and that no-one in the public sector or in a publicly funded organisation should be rewarded for failure?

I must say at the outset that there's a real irony here, isn't there, that the Conservatives choose to focus on high salaries when tax cuts for the highest earners are always among the driving forces of the Conservatives' agenda, which does nothing whatsoever to help people in Wales who are living with the challenges of the cost-of-living crisis.

Across the public sector, we need to make sure that we have the right people in the right place. That does absolutely involve paying them the right sums of money. contributions.text_english:
First Minister, taxpayers don't measure Government efficiency by how many strategies, reviews or initiatives you announce; they measure it by what actually improves and what it costs them.

Your Government has promised measurable outcomes, progress milestones, plans for plans, greater productivity and so on, so will you actually put the numbers against those promises? Will you publish clear targets showing how much taxpayers' money you intend to save, and which areas of Government will become more efficient and by when? And when programmes or public bodies repeatedly fail to deliver value for money, will you actually reform, merge or scrap them? Because Government efficiency cannot just mean spending more money more efficiently; sometimes, it actually means having to spend less.

contributions.text_english: Well, neither does spending less mean that you are being more efficient or more effective, that's what my response would be to that. You spend what you need to spend, not a penny more. You drive that efficiency, you drive that effectiveness. That's the programme that the Government is engaged with now in looking at budgets for the coming years. We have a set budget. Reform voted against fair funding for Wales, but we will work within the budget that we have. And in spending every pound sensibly, in looking at how we get the most out of every pound, that is how we drive outcomes. Because I absolutely agree with the Member that it's not measuring how much you spend, it's what you do with the money. And that also goes on whether you're putting efficiency drives in place for ideological reasons, or whether you're doing it in order to get more out of the system. Let's focus on what we're trying to achieve always for the people of Wales.

contributions.text_english: Effective Government is underpinned by taking a collaborative, cross-sector and holistic approach to policy development and decision making. It recognises that many of the challenges facing Wales cannot be addressed by individual departments working in isolation. Because for too long, previous Governments have operated in silos, failing to look at the bigger picture and tackle shared challenges through joined-up action. Take prevention, for example. Prevention cuts across health, housing and culture. Food policy connects social justice, public health and rural resilience. Creating high-quality jobs needs co-ordination between the economy and education. So, Prif Weinidog, I'd like to know how this Plaid Cymru Welsh Government is already working collaboratively across ministerial portfolios in a tangible and measurable way that will genuinely make a difference to the lives of the people of Wales.

contributions.text_english:
This is a programme of work that we put in place in the early weeks of this new Government. The programme for government is built around a set of priorities. To deliver on those priorities and all those other areas that the Welsh Government is responsible for will take a whole-Government approach. Cross-Government working we really want to be a part of our DNA as a Government.

I tasked the Cabinet Minister for Government effectiveness to ensure that the Government works collectively across portfolios to deliver meaningful outcomes. Here are three examples. On climate change, yes, there's a Minister responsible, but it belongs to all of us, so we've put the structures in place to make sure that we're working collaboratively on climate change. Prevention is another one that cuts across the work of so many departments. Tackling poverty is another one of those.

I'd also make the point, Llywydd, that it's not how we work co-operatively within Government alone that matters. Effective delivery also depends on strong collaboration with others—local government, for example, businesses, the third sector and, crucially, communities across Wales.

contributions.text_english: First Minister, you've spoken about the importance of improving the efficiency and effectiveness of the Welsh Government. You've even appointed a Minister for the task. My constituents and the people of Wales need more than just warm words, new strategies and talking shops. They actually want to see improvements in the areas that matter most to them and they want to see their money spent wisely. Thank you.

contributions.text_english:
First Minister, I accept the health visitor dispute began before you took office, but it has continued under your Government, affecting vulnerable children and families in my constituency. In March, Heledd Fychan, who now sits in your Cabinet, asked the previous First Minister to intervene. Luke Fletcher reminded the Government that it was, in his words,

'setting the policy and funding the services.'

Then, on 17 April, you signed a letter calling for band 6 health visitors to be upgraded to band 7. Yet your Cabinet Minister for health continues to describe this as a local employment dispute between Unite and the health board, with no fixed timetable for resolution. First Minister, you now set the policy, you fund the services, and you signed the call for band 7. So, I ask you plainly: will your Government provide the funding necessary to deliver band 7 for these health visitors? 'Yes' or 'no'?

What we can do in Government is ensure that there is real clarity on roles and bands and pay structures nationally, and that is exactly what the review instigated by the Cabinet Minister for health is setting out to do.

contributions.text_english: Prif Weinidog, I think it's important to challenge the suggestion that nothing has been done on this issue. Plaid Cymru Members have repeatedly raised the dispute with the health board in the Senedd and through the Health and Social Care Committee. The health Minister has engaged with both sides and consistently called for a resolution. The Minister has also been clear that this is not a dispute he can simply impose a settlement on, and the frustration felt by the health visitors is shared across this Chamber. What this long-running dispute does raise, however, is wider concerns about governance and accountability. When concerns can persist for years despite scrutiny and repeated calls for resolution, we must ask whether the warning signs should have been identified much earlier. What lessons is the Government drawing more widely about strengthening leadership and accountability across NHS Wales to prevent disputes reaching this stage in future? Diolch.

At the start of September, my mother passed away. She had spent her entire career working as a health visitor. For her, this work wasn't just a job, it was her calling. My mum's identity, from when she first started training in 1951, was shaped around her time as a health visitor. Even in retirement, you could tell from the way that she spoke and interacted with people that being a health visitor was really part of who she was and what she was meant to be doing. This is the case for so many people for whom their career is a vocation.

Does the First Minister agree with me that, very often, when a career is a vocation for a person, they are often not remunerated according to the value of the kind of work they do for society or in comparison with other equivalent professions? And furthermore, does the First Minister agree that this is an issue that disproportionately affects professions dominated by women, like health visiting, more than it does professions dominated by men?

contributions.text_english: 5. What action is the Welsh Government taking to improve access to essential public services in town and city centres across Wales? OQ64706
contributions.text_original: 5. Pa gamau mae Llywodraeth Cymru yn eu cymryd i wella mynediad at wasanaethau cyhoeddus hanfodol yng nghanol trefi a dinasoedd ledled Cymru? OQ64706

contributions.text_english: The Government believes in the future of our town and city centres. They're at the heart of local identities, our culture and our communities. We refuse to accept their decline and want to reinvent and repurpose those town and city centres for the future. Public services are very much part of that. We want our town and city centres to be places where people can easily access the services they need. We're also investing in better transport links and regeneration schemes and using our town centre taskforce to consider what further action is needed.

contributions.text_english: Diolch, First Minister. Strong cities and towns depend not only on attracting investment but also on ensuring that people can continue to access essential services they rely on every day. In Swansea, the city centre post office in the Quadrant is due to close in February 2027. While a replacement is being explored, no new location or opening date has been confirmed, and the alternative branches do not provide the same range of services. For older residents, disabled people and many small businesses, that would represent a significant loss. First Minister, your Government has rightly committed to supporting thriving high streets and regenerating our towns and city centres. How will the Welsh Government work with partners to safeguard access to essential services, including a full-service post office, as part of a wider regeneration plan for Swansea city centre and communities across Wales?

Across Wales, we will continue to support co-location, accessible transport and business rates relief, which we announced recently, so that regeneration sustains the kind of everyday services that communities rely on, and, at the same time, attracting, hopefully, new investment into these town and city centres.

contributions.text_english:
Thank you, First Minister. I know you've spoken about this earlier, but it's one of those things that I think is going to crop up again and again and again for the next few years, because everyone in this Chamber knows the issues on the M4 around Newport all too well, yet too few of us here acknowledge there is only one proper solution, and that is a relief road.

Some of the alternative suggestions, such as junction closures, are certainly very concerning, and would see huge volumes of traffic pushed into the city, Newport, stifling the local economy there, which is of great concern to many people already, and I know the Minister will be talking to people over the coming months, but there is concern.

And the suggestion to encourage HGVs to use the A465 will supposedly reduce traffic on the M4 by 1 per cent. Now, that's great, but it will then move that same 1 per cent on to already challenged areas like the Hardwick interchange at Abergavenny, which, based on traffic this week, is really, really struggling to cope.

So, let's not send Newport's congestion on a sightseeing tour of Wales. We know the answer is a relief road, First Minister. I note your earlier answer, but if the smaller engineering fixes don't solve the congestion problem—

contributions.text_english:
The Member is referring to what was known as the black route, of course. It is no longer a protected route. When the decision was taken to cancel that particular route, that option was essentially taken off the table, or at least for a very, very, very long time, and we're not prepared to wait that long. And I think we've made it clear that we do think road relief is a part of the solution, and that is why we need to do that careful planning and engineering work to make sure that we understand what is the best solution to pursue, because it's become very, very clear to me—and I've been personally engaged on this, because I have an interest in unblocking this issue for the people of Newport and for the wider south Wales economy—that it will take a host of different things. It will mean—and this is good news for the people of Newport—strengthening public transport. It is important, it will contribute.

Taking traffic on other roads where there is capacity is something that's very, very important, and it could be something as simple as making sure that we provide better provision for HGV drivers, something that I know from my own constituency, with how important that is around Holyhead. So, what I say is, this is live now, this is happening. We're pressing ahead with a multiphase scheme that will crucially take into consideration the views of, and will happen in partnership with, the people of Newport. Will there be challenges in this transformation to a twenty-second century Newport? Yes, but we want to face those challenges and put solutions in place with the people of that city, because there is a city and a broader region that have a lot to benefit from getting this right. Inaction is what we saw up until now; that's not an option now.

contributions.text_english:
Diolch, First Minister. In Fflint Wrecsam, cross-border healthcare is an everyday reality. The Health and Social Care Committee heard evidence a couple of weeks ago that patients can face different waiting time arrangements depending on which side of the border they are treated, that some are left chasing records, test results and appointments themselves, and that there are concerns Welsh patients could become invisible as the NHS in England restructures.

So, with more than 13,000 Welsh patients registered with English general practitioners and over 20,000 English patients registered with Welsh GPs, what concrete assurances can you give that cross-border patients will not face longer waits, poorer co-ordination or unclear accountability when things go wrong? And will your Government commit to publishing regular data on cross-border waiting times, complaints and patient outcomes so that patients don't fall through the gaps?

contributions.text_english:
I'm very glad that the Member pointed out that statistic about traffic for primary care and in which direction it goes. And it's a little-known fact that there are more people from England coming into Wales to see a GP than the other way around. What that tells me is that we need to get this right for people on both sides of the border. I'm a patient in the north of Wales too. It is part of our landscape that there are elements of care that we might get at a specialist children's hospital in Liverpool or a neurosurgery department at Walton and so on. We are committed to making sure that we improve that cross-border working.

I'll give you an example on information sharing: we are working on improving the transfer of referrals, improving the sharing of clinical records, test results and prescribing information. Digital interoperability work is focused on making sure that care becomes safer, becomes more co-ordinated, reducing the need for patients to chase information and so on. In terms of those waiting times, the key thing is that it is the patients that we look after and make sure that we trace their journey through the NHS, wherever that treatment takes place, and for many patients, parts of their treatment will be in the north of Wales and parts of it will be in the north-west of England.

Diolch. I recently visited the Salvation Army in Rhyl, an open-access organisation with a welcoming home-from-home feel, offering a warm space alongside physical and emotional support to anyone seeking help. I was privileged to speak with two amazing volunteers, Chris and Mandy. Both have experienced their own journeys through recovery and now use their lived experiences to support others. Their experiences, alongside those of the others that were there, with accessing services highlighted to me significant challenges individuals experiencing addiction can face when trying to access and retain support. Chaotic living circumstances, mental health difficulties, fear, shame and the physical and cognitive effects of substance use can make it difficult for people to engage with rigid appointment times, overly structured recovery programmes and services that may not accommodate the reality of their lives.

The stigma faced by people experiencing addiction can further hinder recovery, and this stigma doesn't always disappear when in recovery. How can the Government build on the support being offered in Wales to ensure that people experiencing addiction have access to more effective support, and what work can be done to reduce the stigma around addiction?

contributions.text_english: Well, we certainly do recognise the challenges faced by people recovering from addiction, and we value the vital contribution of organisations such as the Salvation Army in supporting recovery. We also recognise, absolutely, the stigma that can be a significant barrier to individuals seeking help and sustaining recovery afterwards. Through investment in local treatment and recovery services, we're working to make sure that people can access the right support at the right time. The Deputy Minister for Public and Preventative Health will continue to engage with people with lived experience, service providers and the wider sectors, so that we can be properly informed as a Government of future action in these areas.

Diolch, Brif Weinidog. There are currently over 10,000 people in temporary accommodation across Wales, including over 2,000 children. I welcome that the Government has set out its ambition to deliver 20,000 new social homes by the end of this Senedd. However, the latest data from Shelter Cymru suggests that there at least 94,000 households currently on a waiting list for a social home.

Will the First Minister commit to publishing a new housing strategy as soon as possible, including the Government's plans for ending homelessness? What steps will you be taking to ensure that everyone in Wales is supported to access a safe and affordable home?

I appreciate the work that the Member does around the issue of housing. Some of the statistics that he mentions are pretty sobering, and we are under no illusion as a Government as to the scale of the challenge that we are facing.

We propose to address this, and look forward to co-operating with him and others on this. We propose to take action, not only in making sure the necessary investment goes in on building more social homes, but that we legislate too, that we put legislative steps in place to make sure that we are emphasising our belief as a Government that people should have that fundamental support in making sure that they have a roof over their heads and somewhere to live safely. This is something that I know drives my housing Cabinet Minister every day in her work.

Trefnydd, I'd be grateful if we could have a statement from the Welsh Government on its overview of local authorities across Wales. A special investigation by the Cambrian News in my constituency has unearthed a number of troubling concerns regarding Ceredigion County Council and its purchase of Llettytwppa Farm, including questions over governance and oversight, allegations of conflict of interest, and the use of significant sums of public money for a project that reportedly has attracted only a small number of students.

Now, I believe that, given the serious nature of the concerns, it's vital that there is a statement from the Welsh Government outlining what oversight mechanisms are available to ensure proper governance and accountability of local authorities in Wales, and to confirm whether the Welsh Government believes any further investigation is warranted in this particular case. The people of my constituency need assurances that public funds are being spent appropriately by the local authority and that decisions are being taken transparently and appropriately. So, I'd be grateful if a statement could be issued by the Welsh Government on this important issue as soon as possible.

contributions.text_english: Certainly. You will have heard the Cabinet Minister talking about the advantages, but also the risks, of AI, and, certainly, there is a recognition, in terms of a number of sectors, when it comes to those risks to jobs that could be lost entirely, or skills. For example, in my portfolio, in terms of music, actors and so on, there are a number of concerns. We're also looking at what the advantages are, and we want that advantage. contributions.text_english: Trefnydd, I'd like to request a statement from the First Minister on the Welsh Government's overseas offices—the network of 20 offices across 11 countries, with an annual running cost of around £4.7 million. Members from more than one party have asked since 2021 for office-by-office costs and benefits, most recently David Mills, on 6 October. The Government has said it cannot break them down. In February, the Government told the Economy, Trade and Rural Affairs Committee it would not release office-by-office investment results, citing data protection and Office for National Statistics rules, and offered only network-wide figures. A Senedd committee has also reported that written information on the wider £58 million international budget was frequently incomplete and unclear, with irreconcilable amounts. Will the Trefnydd ask the First Minister to make a statement on this?

contributions.text_english: I think it is very important that the Member should reflect on which Government you're referring to. You're talking about the Labour Government in your contribution there, whereas we are a new Government, in post since May. So, many of the questions were raised through scrutiny—and I was a member of the committee that undertook that scrutiny work—of the previous Government. Work is ongoing, and is being led by the First Minister, in terms of a new international strategy, which is looking at all of the offices, and looking at how we as a Government engage internationally too. He's been very clear that he wants us to be a Government that engages on the international stage because of the benefits to Wales of doing so. As the work on the strategy is updated, of course, there will be opportunities for Members to be questioning the First Minister and to be engaging and scrutinising.

Can I call for two statements today, please? Can I have a statement in relation to the noise assessment work that needs to be done on the A55 in the Llanddulas area from the Deputy Minister for Transport? This is a priority area for noise reduction. Residents in that community have lived with lots of noise from the A55 for many years. We've been told that a noise assessment is going to be done, but there's no indication as to the timeline for that work or when any follow-up work might be completed, in terms of capital investment for noise barriers. So, I think it is something that I would like an update from the Minister on.

Secondly, can I call for a statement from the Cabinet Minister for Health and Care in relation to medical speciality training for next year? I've been contacted by a group of doctors who are internationally trained, who have many years of experience in the Welsh NHS and want to go on to further their careers, but their experience in the NHS is not currently recognised within the framework as giving them priority access to that training. I do think this is something that the Welsh Government could take action on to address some of the gaps in our workforce in the NHS, and I'd be grateful for a statement.

contributions.text_english: Can I ask for a statement from the Deputy Minister for Transport on Network Rail's plans to close the railway between Holyhead and Chester for four weeks in January to carry out repair works along the line? This is a line that thousands of people rely on, and therefore the impact that this will have on passengers in Bangor Conwy Môn and north Wales will be significant. However, many people who use these services regularly remain unaware of the disruption that lies ahead. I'm pleased to see that Network Rail has now published further information about the work, but I would like to request a statement from the Deputy Minister outlining the support that the Welsh Government can provide between now and January to spread the word, ensuring that local residents are aware of the situation and have the opportunity to make alternative travel arrangements. Thank you.
contributions.text_original: Gaf i ofyn am ddatganiad gan y Dirprwy Weinidog dros Drafnidiaeth ar gynlluniau Network Rail i gau'r rheilffordd rhwng Caergybi a Chaer am bedair wythnos ym mis Ionawr er mwyn cynnal gwaith atgyweirio ar hyd y llinell? Mae hwn yn rheilffordd y mae miloedd o bobl yn ddibynnol arno, ac felly bydd yr effaith y bydd hyn yn ei chael ar deithwyr ym Mangor Conwy Môn a gogledd Cymru yn sylweddol. Serch hynny, mae nifer fawr o bobl sy'n defnyddio'r gwasanaethau yma yn rheolaidd yn parhau yn anymwybodol o'r tarfu sydd o'u blaenau. Dwi'n falch o weld bod Network Rail erbyn hyn wedi cyhoeddi rhagor o ddeunydd gwybodaeth am y gwaith, ond hoffwn ofyn am ddatganiad gan y Dirprwy Weinidog sy'n gosod allan y gefnogaeth y gall Llywodraeth Cymru ei rhoi rhwng rŵan a mis Ionawr i ledaenu'r gair, fel bod trigolion lleol yn ymwybodol o'r sefyllfa ac yn cael cyfle i baratoi cynlluniau teithio amgen. Diolch.

But, just to reassure you, the Welsh Government is engaging with Network Rail and Avanti and Transport for Wales through network north Wales meetings, and Transport for Wales and Avanti are completing detailed plans for bus replacement services during that closure period as well.
contributions.text_original: Diolch i'r Aelod am godi'r mater hwn. Rwy'n gwerthfawrogi y bydd hyn yn creu aflonyddwch o ran y gwasanaeth dros dro i deithwyr tra bydd y rheilffordd ar gau. Mae'r Dirprwy Weinidog dros Drafnidiaeth eisoes wedi cyhoeddi datganiad ysgrifenedig. Os oes yna unrhyw bryderon ychwanegol, mi fyddwn i'n eich annog chi i ysgrifennu at yr Aelod. contributions.text_english: Business Manager, can I ask for a joint statement from the Deputy Minister for social care, the Minister for local government and the Minister for education on the pupil development grant for children looked after? The issue I raise is complicated and cuts across multiple portfolios. A recent Estyn report highlighted concerns about the current PDG-CLA funding arrangements. Corporate parenting responsibility remains with the placing authority, but the receiving authorities are required to provide support from their own PDG-CLA allocation. Estyn also reported existing arrangements did not always operate effectively, including inconsistent information sharing and joint working, particularly when learners move between settings, services and local authorities. So, can I have a statement on how the Welsh Government intends to address these issues highlighted in Estyn's report? Diolch.

contributions.text_english: I thank the Member for that question. In terms of a statement, it's not the norm to have a joint statement in that way. We do work across Government, of course, and certainly, if you were to write to the Ministers with specific questions, then you would receive that response. But, clearly, the Cabinet Minister for education leads on the pupil development grant, but there is close collaboration between Ministers where there is that overlap. What is important is that we do have that co-operation, because what we're trying to do is to always respond to Estyn recommendations. There is work, of course, for the relevant scrutiny committees in this Senedd and the cross-party group to be looking at such issues, to ensure that implementation is as it should be and that recommendations made by Estyn are progressed.
contributions.text_original: Diolch i'r Aelod am y cwestiwn hwnnw. O ran y datganiad, dydy o ddim yn arferol i gael datganiad ar y cyd yn y modd hwnnw. Mae yna waith, wrth gwrs, i'r pwyllgorau craffu priodol yn y Senedd hon a grŵp trawsbleidiol i fod yn edrych ar faterion o'r fath, a sicrhau bod y gweithrediad fel y dylai fod a bod argymhellion sy'n cael eu gwneud gan Estyn yn mynd rhagddynt.

contributions.text_english: Prynhawn da, Drefnydd. I want a statement, please, on the services for women, in particular in rural areas, when they face domestic violence. Last week, two cases in Wales were in our media. In Carmarthen, James McKenna was jailed for 24 years for the attempted murder of his ex-partner, whom he stalked and stabbed repeatedly as she walked her dog. And secondly, there's the really tragic case in Prestatyn, of mother of four Samantha Phythian, who was pregnant and found dead in a burning van. All of these cases, along with the cases of women who are living in rural areas that I represent, show how hard it is for those women to get the services and the responses they need. Could you please give us an update and a statement, and perhaps from the Minister as well, on services for women who face domestic violence and what you're doing to develop these and ensure that they reach everybody? Diolch yn fawr iawn.

contributions.text_english: I thank the Member for raising this issue, which received a lot of attention in the press last week, and I would like to say how brave those people who are speaking out about these things are, and it is terrible to hear about that suffering. The Deputy First Minister is here and will have heard what you've raised, and I would like to give you that assurance that we do acknowledge this, that the recent review of the national VAWDASV strategy has noted rural inequality as a key theme in terms of this work. contributions.text_english: Trefnydd, I would like a statement from the Government regarding the threat to our most valuable industry, tourism. In Carmarthenshire, tourism earned, in 2024-25, £724 million, employing over 6,600 full-time employees. This is vital to Wales's economy, and we need to listen to the challenge it is facing. I believe this Government doesn't appear to be listening. A whole raft of taxation and regulation is having a serious impact on these businesses. Let's talk about the visitor levy, a tourist tax that is placing another burden on the industry. We are now faced with plans to turn Wales into a giant energy park, with hundreds of enormous wind turbines and pylons in our most beautiful countryside that attracts millions of visitors. Are you aware of the impact? Are you listening to the tourism industry? And what action are you taking to protect it? Diolch.

contributions.text_english: Well, tourism is hugely important for the Welsh economy, and the Member, I'm sure, will be aware that there are a number of challenges that have been faced by that sector, including the cost-of-living crisis. People have less money in their pockets. There is also the impact of Brexit, which has had an impact on the number of visitors to Wales and to our communities. You're referring to an area that is not implementing the tourism levy at the moment and referring to that as a barrier, and I don't really understand that. We have to look at the facts as they are. Every area will have its own challenges. We also know that there are opportunities that come with some of the things that are in train. But what we are committed to is ensuring that we work with Visit Wales to sell Wales to the world, that we want to ensure that tourism can prosper and that we support those businesses. It is central as regards what was in our manifesto and to the work that we are looking at on a cross-ministerial basis. As a Government, I, as Minister with responsibility for culture and sport, also believe that we're not taking full advantage of the tourism related to our history, our culture, and the opportunities that comes with major events such as the Tour de France and the Euros in 2028. Therefore, tourism is hugely important to this Government and we are working on a cross-ministerial basis on it.
contributions.text_original: Wel, mae twristiaeth yn bwysig ofnadwy o ran economi Cymru, ac mi fydd yr Aelod, dwi'n siŵr, yn gwybod bod yna nifer fawr o heriau sydd wedi wynebu'r sector hwnnw, gan gynnwys yr argyfwng costau byw. Mae gan bobl lai o arian yn eu pocedi. Mae Brexit hefyd, er enghraifft, wedi cael effaith ar nifer y bobl sy'n dod i Gymru a'n cymunedau ni. Rydych chi'n cyfeirio at ardal sydd ddim yn mynd rhagddo efo'r lefi twristiaeth ar y funud, gan nodi hwnna fel rhwystr, a dwi ddim yn deall hynny. Mae'n rhaid i ni edrych ar y ffeithiau. Mi fydd pob ardal efo'i heriau gwahanol. Rydyn ni hefyd yn gwybod bod yna gyfleon yn dod efo rhai o'r pethau sydd mewn grym. Ond yr hyn rydyn ni wedi ymrwymo iddo fo ydy sicrhau ein bod ni'n gweithio gyda Chroeso Cymru i werthu Cymru i'r byd, ein bod ni eisiau sicrhau bod twristiaeth yn gallu ffynnu a'n bod ni'n cefnogi'r busnesau hynny. Mae o'n ganolog o ran yr hyn rydyn ni wedi ei roi yn ein maniffesto ni a'r gwaith rydyn ni'n edrych yn drawsweinidigol arno fo. Dwi, fel Gweinidog efo cyfrifoldeb dros ddiwylliant a chwaraeon, hefyd yn credu nad ydyn ni'n manteisio i'r eithaf o ran y dwristiaeth sy'n gysylltiedig efo'n hanes ni, efo'n diwylliant ni, a'r cyfleoedd sydd yn dod efo digwyddiadau mawr, fel y Tour de France, fel yr Ewros yn dod yn 2028. Felly, mae twristiaeth yn bwysig iawn i'r Llywodraeth hon ac rydyn ni'n gweithio'n drawsweinidogol ar hynny.

contributions.text_english: Trefnydd, I'd like to request a statement on transport accessibility for blind and partially sighted people from the Deputy Minister for Transport to understand what more can be done to ensure everyone can travel safely, confidently and independently. Last week, I had the privilege of spending the morning with Rachel from the Royal National Institute of Blind People and her guide dog, Flick, as we attempted to walk from the bus station in Wrexham to the train station. I was provided a pair of goggles to help me understand Rachel's visual impairment. What struck me was the daily challenges facing people with sight loss in navigating their surroundings and accessing public transport. Access to public transport is essential for people to maintain their independence, access healthcare and stay connected to their communities. It's important that buses, trains and transport infrastructure are accessible, and that people with sight loss feel safe when travelling, certainly to avoid any risk of isolation. So, I'd be grateful for a statement from the Deputy Minister to highlight the work undertaken by the Welsh Government to ensure that blind and partially sighted people can access this transport as easily as possible. Thank you.

contributions.text_english: Trefnydd, I would like to request an urgent Government statement on the independence, accountability and powers of Care Inspectorate Wales. When social services fail, accountability cannot be optional. Section 150 of Social Services and Well-being (Wales) Act 2014 sets out clear statutory grounds for intervention where a local authority fails, or is likely to fail, in the exercise of its social services functions. Section 152 then gives Welsh Ministers the power to intervene where statutory conditions aren't met. Yet, Care Inspectorate Wales exercises its functions on behalf of Welsh Ministers. That raises a serious question about whether professional independence goes far enough. Families affected by serious failures deserve a regulator whose structural independence is beyond question, with powers necessary to expose systematic problems and ensure they are acted upon. Will the Government, therefore, bring forward an urgent statement setting out precisely how it will ensure that Care Inspectorate Wales can make decisions independently of Welsh Ministers, while remaining fully transparent and accountable to the people of Wales and the Senedd? Diolch.

Dwi ddim yn gwybod os ydych chi wedi ysgrifennu at y Gweinidog Cabinet gyda'r pryderon penodol—yn amlwg, mewn munud, mae'n anodd i chi roi'r holl wybodaeth hynny. Ond, yn sicr, os oes yna bryderon y mae angen i ni eu hystyried, wrth gwrs y gwnawn ni hynny fel Llywodraeth. Felly, byddwn ni yn gofyn i chi wneud hynny.

contributions.text_english: Business Minister, can I please request an urgent statement from the Welsh Government about the proposed closure of the three junctions alongside the M4 in Newport? All residents know that shutting down junctions 27, 26 and 25 on the M4 would be disastrous and cause nothing but chaos and mayhem across the city, with traffic being pushed into already congested routes. Now, news of the Government's junction closure plans has sparked anger and uproar in Newport, with constituents inundating me and other MSs with e-mails, calls and also letters. The message is clear: they want the Government to keep their hands off our motorway junctions. And I've spoken to numerous constituents living near junction 27 who've told me that they're seriously considering moving and selling up because they just can't handle what's going to be coming their way. And it's not just residents and businesses who have serious concerns over the Government plans. Gwent police and crime commissioner has warned that these closures could pose a serious risk to our emergency service response times, going forward. The Government has insisted that it will listen to the concerns and voice of those directly impacted by these plans, but we haven't heard how exactly this is going to be achieved. So, an urgent statement from the Government outlining its plans, how it's going to be consulting with residents, businesses and emergency services, as well as others, and when this work will start, is urgently needed by us all. Thank you.

contributions.text_english:
I hope that the Member heard the oral statement last week. I don't think there has been a lack of opportunity to scrutinise and to ask the Minister questions. So, I don't think that a statement so soon after that is appropriate, in particular because, let's bear in mind, of what was noted, which was that we're now going to be looking at considering the evidence, understanding the different facts and options, and working towards solutions that improve journeys whilst supporting communities, businesses and the broader economy. So, as to all of the concerns that you have set out, that's exactly what will be happening now: listening.

I'm sure as well that the Member—like all Members here, I hope—wants to see this Government taking action. We have seen 27 years of a lack of action and a lack of solutions, so we have to move forward with this work. The engagement work is happening at the moment, and everyone with concerns has an opportunity to be part of this. It was announced last week that there would be more updates and opportunities for people to be engaging. So, I hope that we will be able to unite behind the fact that the Minister has outlined a way forward finally, and there will be an opportunity for those who have concerns to express those. But we do have to see a solution. I'm sure the Member agrees with me on that.

Dwi'n gobeithio bod yr Aelod wedi clywed y datganiad llafar yr wythnos diwethaf. Dwi ddim yn meddwl bod yna ddiffyg cyfle wedi bod i graffu a holi'r Gweinidog. Felly, dwi ddim yn meddwl bod datganiad mor fuan wedi hynny yn briodol, yn arbennig oherwydd, beth am inni gofio, beth oedd yr hyn a nodwyd, sef ein bod ni rŵan yn mynd i fod yn edrych ar ystyried y dystiolaeth, deall y ffeithiau a'r gwahanol opsiynau, a gweithio tuag at ddatrysiadau sy'n gwella teithiau wrth gefnogi cymunedau, busnesau a'r economi ehangach. Felly, o ran yr holl bryderon rydych chi wedi'u nodi, dyna'n union beth fydd yn digwydd rŵan: gwrando.

Dwi'n siŵr hefyd fod yr Aelod—fel pob Aelod yma, gobeithio—eisiau gweld y Llywodraeth hon yn gweithredu. Rydyn ni wedi gweld 27 mlynedd o beidio â gweithredu a chael datrysiadau, felly mae'n rhaid inni symud ymlaen efo'r gwaith hwn. Mae'r gwaith ymgysylltu yn mynd rhagddo. Mae yna gyfle i bawb sydd efo pryderon i fod yn rhan o hyn. Mi gyhoeddwyd yr wythnos diwethaf y bydd yna ragor o ddiweddariadau ac mi fydd yna gyfle i bobl ymgysylltu. Felly, dwi'n gobeithio ein bod ni'n gallu uno yn y ffaith bod y Gweinidog wedi amlinellu ffordd ymlaen o'r diwedd, a bydd yna gyfle i'r rheini sydd efo pryderon i fynegi'r rheini. Ond mae'n rhaid inni weld datrysiad. Dwi'n siŵr bod yr Aelod yn gytûn ar hynny.

contributions.text_english: Good afternoon, Trefnydd. Since questioning the First Minister on NHS dental care last week, I have had countless constituents and people across Wales get in contact. One said that they have waited unsuccessfully since 2019 to get back on an NHS list, now facing £800-plus for root canal treatment. Another says they finally secured NHS care, only to be restricted to emergency treatment due to the new dental contract. Another says their practice has gone private, demanding £264 a year just for membership fees. This is the reality of your fundamentally flawed dental contract. A new dental school is welcome, of course it is, but it is the contract that needs reworking, and this Government needs to listen, as I said last week, to practising dentists to make the contract fit for purpose. A lack of NHS dental care is now a national emergency, and I believe this requires an urgent statement on the floor of this Senedd or a debate to address this. Diolch.

contributions.text_english:
Diolch, Ddirprwy Lywydd. Today, I am updating Members on the next steps regarding the Glyndŵr National Park (Designation) Order submitted to Welsh Ministers by Natural Resources Wales in January of this year.

Following careful consideration of the designation Order, the evidence assembled by Natural Resources Wales, the representations and objections received during the designation process, and the associated impact assessments, I have reached a provisional view in respect of the question of whether to confirm, confirm with modifications or to reject the designation Order. I am currently minded not to confirm the designation Order, and consequently minded not to proceed with a public local inquiry at this stage. Not confirming the designation Order and not proceeding with a public local inquiry will mean that no new national park is established at this time.

I do want to be clear with Members that this is not a final decision. Before reaching a final decision, I intend to provide a short opportunity for everyone with an interest in this proposal to make further representations in respect of the provisional view that I have reached.

contributions.text_english:
Members will be aware that the previous administration asked Natural Resources Wales to assess the case for a new national park. Following an extensive programme of evidence gathering, engagement and consultation, NRW concluded that the area comprising the proposed Glyndŵr national park did meet the statutory tests for designation, and submitted the designation Order to Welsh Ministers.

Since then, a significant volume of evidence has been gathered. Over 400 responses were received during the notification period. These reflected a variety of views, with many respondents supporting the proposal and many opposing it. Significant objections were also submitted, including objections from every one of the five local authorities in the area. There were strong feelings in favour and strong feelings against. Many have highlighted the potential benefits: these include opportunities to enhance nature recovery, strengthen climate resilience, provide strategic leadership for landscape management, and support recreation and sustainable tourism. The evidence presented by NRW identifies a number of opportunities in these areas.

At the same time, important questions have been raised throughout the process relating to affordability, funding requirements in the future, value for money, governance arrangements and potential impacts on local communities, infrastructure, energy developments, housing and the Welsh language. These concerns have been raised by local authorities, businesses and land managers.

In reaching my provisional view, I have carefully considered these issues. I have considered the findings of the regulatory impact assessment and integrated impact assessment prepared by officials. That analysis highlights both possible benefits and significant uncertainties. The regulatory impact assessment estimates establishment costs of over £11 million and identifies ongoing costs associated with establishing and operating a new national park authority. It also notes uncertainty in the evidence base.

Bydd Aelodau'n cofio bod y weinyddiaeth flaenorol wedi gofyn i Gyfoeth Naturiol Cymru i asesu'r achos o blaid parc cenedlaethol newydd. Yn dilyn rhaglen drwyadl o gasglu tystiolaeth, trafod ac ymgynghori, daeth Cyfoeth Naturiol Cymru i'r casgliad bod ardal y parc cenedlaethol Glyndŵr arfaethedig yn bodloni'r profion statudol ar gyfer ei dynodi, a chyflwynodd Orchymyn dynodi i Weinidogion Cymru.

Ers hynny, mae llwyth o dystiolaeth wedi'i chasglu. Daeth dros 400 o ymatebion i law yn ystod y cyfnod hysbysu. Roedd y rhain yn adlewyrchu amrywiaeth o safbwyntiau, gyda llawer o ymatebwyr yn cefnogi a llawer yn gwrthwynebu. Cyflwynwyd gwrthwynebiadau sylweddol hefyd, gan gynnwys gwrthwynebiadau gan bob un o'r pum awdurdod lleol yn yr ardal berthnasol. Teimladau cryf o blaid a theimladau cryf yn erbyn. Mae llawer wedi tynnu sylw at y manteision posibl: cyfleoedd i adfer natur, gwrthsefyll newid hinsawdd yn well, rhoi arweiniad strategol ar gyfer rheoli'r dirwedd, cefnogi hamddena a thwristiaeth gynaliadwy. Mae'r dystiolaeth gan Gyfoeth Naturiol Cymru yn nodi nifer o gyfleoedd yn y meysydd hyn.

Ar yr un pryd, mae cwestiynau pwysig wedi'u codi ar hyd y broses yn ymwneud â fforddiadwyedd, gofynion cyllidol y dyfodol, gwerth am arian, trefniadau llywodraethu ac effeithiau posibl ar gymunedau lleol, seilwaith, datblygiadau ynni, tai a'r iaith Gymraeg. As I have already noted, all five local authorities in the area objected to the designation. While I have carefully considered all representations received, I do recognise the importance of understanding the views of these local authorities, which already play a role in delivering many of the outcomes that are sought through designation and which would be important partners should a national park ultimately be established.

I therefore consider that there is great value in continuing to maintain a strong focus on enabling those existing designations and partnerships to deliver for nature, climate, cultural heritage, recreation and local communities, while continuing to pursue the objectives identified through the Glyndŵr park designation process through other mechanisms. For example, we are taking practical action to restore nature and build climate resilience across the north-east. Through the Welsh Government’s national peatland programme, significant restoration work has been delivered within the Clwydian range and Dee valley national landscape, including at Llandegla moor site, which is of special scientific interest, bringing around 120 hectares of peatland into a more favourable condition.

The evidence demonstrates that many of the challenges identified by Natural Resources Wales are already being addressed through this Welsh Government's current programmes. These include our work on biodiversity recovery, peatland restoration, nature networks, the sustainable farming scheme, including Ffermio Bro, climate and nature action, sustainable tourism and wider rural investment.

Importantly, these policies are already delivering real outcomes for communities, farmers and the environment. Ffermio Bro, our bespoke sustainable farming scheme for designated landscapes, is supporting farmers to deliver practical action for nature recovery, climate resilience and sustainable land management. Farmers at Llangwyfan farm are restoring hedgerows to reconnect ancient woodland and improve woodland management to strengthen habitats for native flora and fauna. This is helping to create a more connected and resilient landscape. It therefore appears to me that the objectives identified through the designation process may be delivered through alternative mechanisms, without establishing a new national park authority and without incurring the ongoing financial commitments that the designation would require.

Looking ahead, I believe there will be further opportunities to secure these outcomes through the Welsh Government's work, through our climate and nature action plan, our culture strategy, our proposed rural-proofing and environmental sustainability duty, which will strengthen the consideration of environmental sustainability, climate resilience and rural impacts across public sector decision making. I will also consider whether existing arrangements for national landscapes can be further strengthened, alongside other integrated approaches that support nature recovery, sustainable land management and thriving rural communities.

Having said all that, I do recognise the significance of this proposal in front of us today and the strong interest it continues to generate. My responsibility is to reach a reasonable conclusion on the basis of all the relevant information. It's for that reason that I am not making a final decision today. Instead, I invite any party to submit further representations before reaching a final decision.

This is therefore an opportunity for local authorities, representative organisations, businesses, community groups and members of the public to present any additional evidence, arguments or material considerations that they believe Welsh Ministers should take into account. People and organisations can submit their views via e-mail or through the post, the details of which will be on the Welsh Government's website as we bring the statement in the Senedd today to a close. I will also be publishing links to a range of evidence that has been developed during the process so far to further inform these considerations. I would encourage people to provide new evidence, in particular, or information that has not already been considered through the extensive work carried out to date.

The intention of these steps is not to repeat earlier consultation exercises; rather, it is intended to ensure that all relevant evidence has been properly considered and in a reasonable manner before a final decision is made. Once this period has concluded, in four weeks' time, officials will analyse the representations received and provide further advice to me. Then I will consider all submissions carefully before coming to a final decision, as well as publishing my reasons.

The landscapes, communities and cultural heritage of the north-east are nationally important. Whatever the final outcome, the evidence assembled over recent years has highlighted both their special qualities and the challenges they face. I remain committed to working with partners to secure positive outcomes for those landscapes, communities and future generations. Note again that this announcement represents a provisional view only. I encourage all interested parties to engage constructively with the next steps so that any final decision is informed by the fullest possible consideration of the evidence before us. Thank you very much.

Fel dwi eisoes wedi'i nodi, gwnaeth y pum awdurdod lleol yn yr ardal wrthwynebu'r dynodiad. Dwi'n ystyried felly fod gwerth mawr mewn parhau i gadw ffocws cryf ar alluogi'r dynodiadau a'r partneriaethau presennol yma i gyflawni ar gyfer natur, hinsawdd, treftadaeth ddiwylliannol, hamdden a chymunedau lleol, tra'n parhau i fynd ar drywydd yr amcanion a nodwyd drwy broses ddynodi parc Glyndŵr drwy fecanweithiau eraill. Er enghraifft, rŷn ni'n cymryd camau ymarferol i adfer natur ac adeiladu gwydnwch hinsawdd ar draws y gogledd-ddwyrain. Drwy raglen genedlaethol mawndir Llywodraeth Cymru, cyflawnwyd gwaith adfer sylweddol o fewn tirwedd genedlaethol bryniau Clwyd a dyffryn Dyfrdwy, gan gynnwys safle rhostir Llandegla sydd o ddiddordeb gwyddonol arbennig, gan ddod â thua 120 hectar o fawndir i gyflwr gwell.

Mae'r dystiolaeth yn dangos bod llawer o'r heriau a nodwyd gan Gyfoeth Naturiol Cymru eisoes dan ystyriaeth gan raglenni presennol y Llywodraeth hon. Yn eu plith mae ein gwaith ar adfer bioamrywiaeth, adfer mawndiroedd, rhwydweithiau natur, y cynllun ffermio cynaliadwy, gan gynnwys Ffermio Bro, gweithredu ar hinsawdd a natur, twristiaeth gynaliadwy a buddsoddi ehangach yng nghefn gwlad.

Yn bwysig, mae'r polisïau yma eisoes yn cyflawni canlyniadau gwirioneddol i gymunedau, ffermwyr a'r amgylchedd. Mae Ffermio Bro, ein cynllun ffermio cynaliadwy pwrpasol ar gyfer tirweddau dynodedig, yn cefnogi ffermwyr i weithredu’n ymarferol ar gyfer adferiad natur, gwydnwch hinsawdd a rheoli tir cynaliadwy. Mae ffermwyr yn fferm Llangwyfan yn adfer gwrychoedd i ailgysylltu coetir hynafol a gwella rheoli coetiroedd i gryfhau cynefinoedd ar gyfer fflora a ffawna brodorol. Mae hyn yn helpu i greu tirwedd fwy cysylltiedig a gwydn. Mae'n ymddangos i mi, felly, y gellir cyflawni'r amcanion a gafodd eu nodi gan y broses ddynodi trwy fecanweithiau amgen, heb sefydlu awdurdod parc cenedlaethol newydd a heb ysgwyddo'r ymrwymiadau ariannol y byddai ar y dynodiad eu hangen wedi hynny.

Wrth edrych ymlaen, dwi'n credu bydd yna gyfleoedd pellach i sicrhau'r canlyniadau hyn drwy waith y Llywodraeth, drwy ein cynllun gweithredu hinsawdd a natur sydd ar ein gweill, ein strategaeth ddiwylliant, ein dyletswydd diogelu gwledig a chynaliadwyedd amgylcheddol arfaethedig, a fydd yn cryfhau'r ystyriaeth o gynaliadwyedd amgylcheddol, gwydnwch hinsawdd ac effeithiau gwledig ar draws penderfyniadau'r sector cyhoeddus. Dwi hefyd am ystyried a ellir cryfhau'r trefniadau presennol ar gyfer tirweddau cenedlaethol, ochr yn ochr â dulliau integredig eraill sy'n cefnogi adferiad natur, rheoli tir cynaliadwy a chymunedau gwledig ffyniannus.

Wedi dweud hynny i gyd, dwi'n cydnabod arwyddocâd y cynnig hwn sydd o'n blaenau heddiw a'r diddordeb mawr sydd ynddo. Fy nghyfrifoldeb i yw dod i gasgliad rhesymol ar sail yr holl wybodaeth berthnasol. Am y rheswm hwnnw, dwi ddim am wneud penderfyniad terfynol heddiw. Yn hytrach, dwi’n gwahodd unrhyw barti i gyflwyno sylwadau pellach cyn inni wneud penderfyniad terfynol.

Dyma gyfle felly i awdurdodau lleol, sefydliadau cynrychioladol, busnesau, grwpiau cymunedol ac aelodau o'r cyhoedd gyflwyno unrhyw dystiolaeth, dadleuon neu ystyriaethau materol ychwanegol y credant y dylai Gweinidogion Cymru eu hystyried. Gall pobl a sefydliadau gyflwyno'u barn drwy e-bost neu drwy'r post, a bydd y manylion ar wefan Llywodraeth Cymru wrth i ni ddod i ddiwedd y datganiad hwn yn y Senedd heddiw. Byddaf hefyd yn cyhoeddi dolenni i ystod o'r dystiolaeth sydd wedi'i ddatblygu yn ystod y broses hyd yma i lywio'r ystyriaethau ymhellach. Byddwn i'n annog pobl i gyflwyno sylwadau yn benodol sy'n darparu tystiolaeth neu wybodaeth newydd nad ydynt eisoes wedi eu hystyried drwy'r gwaith helaeth a wnaed hyd yn hyn.

Nid bwriad y camau hyn yw ailadrodd ymarferion ymgynghori cynharach; yn hytrach, mae'n bwriadu sicrhau bod yr holl dystiolaeth berthnasol wedi ei hystyried yn briodol ac yn rhesymol cyn gwneud penderfyniad terfynol. Ar ôl i'r cyfnod hwn ddod i ben, mewn pedair wythnos, bydd swyddogion yn dadansoddi'r sylwadau a dderbyniwyd ac yn rhoi cyngor pellach i mi. Yna byddaf yn ystyried yr holl gyflwyniadau yn ofalus cyn dod i benderfyniad terfynol, ynghyd â chyhoeddi fy rhesymau.

Mae tirweddau cymunedau a threftadaeth ddiwylliannol y gogledd-ddwyrain yn bwysig yn genedlaethol. Beth bynnag yw'r canlyniad terfynol, mae'r dystiolaeth a gasglwyd dros y blynyddoedd diwethaf wedi tynnu sylw at eu rhinweddau arbennig a'r heriau maen nhw'n eu hwynebu. Dwi'n parhau i ymrwymo i weithio gyda phartneriaid i sicrhau canlyniadau cadarnhaol i'r tirweddau, i'r cymunedau a chenedlaethau'r dyfodol. Nodwch eto: mae'r cyhoeddiad hwn yn cynrychioli barn dros dro yn unig. Dwi'n annog pawb sydd â diddordeb i ymgysylltu'n adeiladol ar y camau nesaf, fel bod unrhyw benderfyniad terfynol yn cael ei lywio gan yr ystyriaeth lawnaf bosib o'r dystiolaeth sydd o'n blaenau. Diolch yn fawr.
