contributions.text_english:
Thank you, Dirprwy Lywydd. I have to say that I do feel this is very encouraging, what we've heard from your statement. It's really good to hear that many of the things that have been put in place in the past are now bearing fruit, such as the national flood forum—that's fantastic. I truly do believe in the power of networks that work across Wales to help each other, so that's fantastic.

I also took notice of what you said in terms of the kind of support we can provide to our communities due to the fact that they have to be vigilant of risk, register for warnings and alerts, be prepared, and receive practical support from NRW. I also feel very privileged to stand here today and to hear everyone speaking about this subject. We all feel very concerned about what's happening with our communities across Wales and across all of the parties, and that's fantastic to hear.

What I want to ask is how can we give that confidence that our communities need that our Government, that we here, are doing everything we can do to ensure that adequate property-level resilience measures are available, and that they're safe.
contributions.text_original:
Diolch, Ddirprwy Lywydd. Mae'n rhaid i fi ddweud, dwi yn teimlo ei fod e'n galonogol iawn, eich datganiad heddiw. Roedd e rili yn dda clywed bod lot o'r pethau sydd wedi cael eu rhoi yn eu lle o'r blaen nawr yn digwydd, fel y fforwm llifogydd cenedlaethol—mae hwnna'n ffantastig. Dwi wir yn credu mewn grym rhwydweithiau sydd yn gweithio ar draws Cymru i helpu ein gilydd a phopeth, so mae hwnna'n ffantastig.

Roeddwn i hefyd yn rili cymryd sylw o beth roeddech chi'n ei ddweud o ran pa fath o gymorth rydyn ni'n gallu ei roi i'n cymunedau ni o ganlyniad i'r ffaith bod yn rhaid iddyn nhw wylio am risg, cofrestru i gael rhybuddion, bod yn barod am unrhyw beth, a chael y cymorth ymarferol gan Cyfoeth Naturiol Cymru. Dwi hefyd yn teimlo'n rili freintiedig i sefyll fan hyn a chlywed pawb yn siarad amdano fe fel hyn. Rŷn ni i gyd yn poeni am beth sydd yn digwydd gyda'n cymunedau ni ar draws Cymru ac ar draws yr holl bleidiau hefyd. So, mae hwnna'n ffantastig.

Beth dwi eisiau gofyn yw sut ydyn ni'n gallu rhoi'r hyder yna sydd ei angen ar ein cymunedau bod ein Llywodraeth ni, ein bod ni fan hyn, yn gwneud popeth rŷn ni'n gallu ei wneud i sicrhau bod mesurau gwydnwch ar lefel eiddo digonol ar gael iddynt, a'u bod nhw'n saff.

contributions.text_english:
Thank you. At a property level, as I mentioned earlier, there is an opportunity to have specific investment for property resilience as a result of flooding, and I would encourage risk management authorities across Wales to bring forward their specific requirements for investments in that regard. I did make reference to the role that insurance companies have to play. Build back better is the name of the scheme. If you've been affected, as part of the insurance work, there are some insurance companies that are willing to invest more than the value of the damage to help prevent further future damage. I would encourage people to speak to their insurers when they face those situations.

I would also say, with the measures looking at specific properties, that it is important that that work is done by appropriate, qualified companies who know what they're doing. That's why we say that risk management authorities are best placed to commission this work, and that the applications should come through them, and then they can ensure that the necessary standards are met. But also, at a community level, they can ensure economies of scale where there are a number of properties being dealt with simultaneously.

I would return to where I started earlier: I see the national flood forum for Wales as a key means of being an advocate for those people who live in those communities that are living under this cloud, holding their hand, working with them to prepare so that they can have greater confidence—if something does happen, that they know what they need to do, and that they will know that some of the measures available to them will make a difference, and if the worst were to happen, that there is someone with them on that appallingly long journey back to recovery. I think that's another important message.
contributions.text_original:
Diolch. Ar lefel eiddo, fel rôn i'n sôn yn gynharach, mae yna gyfle i gael buddsoddiad penodol ar gyfer gwydnwch eiddo yn wyneb llifogydd, a byddwn i'n annog awdurdodau rheoli risg ar draws Cymru i ddod ymlaen gyda gofynion penodol ar gyfer buddsoddiadau yn hynny o beth. Mi wnes i gyfeirio hefyd at rôl sydd gan y cwmnïau yswiriant i chwarae. Build back better yw'r term maen nhw'n ei ddefnyddio. Os ŷch chi wedi cael eich effeithio, fel rhan o'r gwaith yswiriant, mae yna rai cwmnïau yswiriant yn barod i fuddsoddi mwy na gwerth y difrod er mwyn helpu i atal difrod pellach yn y dyfodol. Felly, byddwn i'n annog pobl i siarad â'u cwmnïau yswiriant pan fyddant yn wynebu sefyllfa fel yna.

Byddwn i hefyd yn dweud, gyda'r mesurau sy'n edrych ar eiddo penodol, ei bod hi'n bwysig bod y gwaith yna'n cael ei wneud gan gwmnïau cymwys—cwmnïau sy'n gwybod beth maen nhw'n ei wneud. Dyna pam rŷn ni'n dweud mai'r awdurdodau rheoli risg sydd yn y lle gorau i gomisiynu'r gwaith yma, a bod y ceisiadau'n dod trwyddyn nhw, oherwydd wedyn maen nhw'n gallu sicrhau bod y safonau angenrheidiol yn cael eu cwrdd. Maen nhw hefyd, ar sail gymunedol, yn gallu sicrhau economies of scale lle mae yna sawl eiddo'n cael eu delio â nhw ar yr un pryd.

contributions.text_english: We'll move on now to item 5, a statement by the Cabinet Minister for Health and Care, an update on winter preparedness. I call on the Cabinet Minister for Health and Care, Mabon ap Gwynfor.
contributions.text_original: Symudwn at eitem 5 nawr, datganiad gan y Gweinidog Cabinet dros Iechyd a Gofal, diweddariad ar barodrwydd ar gyfer y gaeaf. Galwaf ar y Gweinidog Cabinet dros Iechyd a Gofal, Mabon ap Gwynfor.

contributions.text_english:
Thank you very much, Llywydd. Today I am setting out the decisive actions that this Government is taking to protect people, to support staff, and to strengthen health and care services across Wales this winter. The winter will be challenging. Demand will rise, respiratory illness will place additional pressure on services, and the constraints in terms of the workforce, finance and social care will remain significant.

We cannot remove every risk, but we can prepare earlier, intervene faster, and require every part of the system to act together. That's why we've acted earlier than any previous Welsh Government, demonstrating stronger national leadership, clearer expectations, and a relentless focus on delivery.

Every health board has submitted its draft winter preparedness plan by 1 September. For the first time, those plans are being stress-tested during September and October so that risks, assumptions and dependencies are challenged, and that action is taken before pressure peaks. This is a material strengthening of our approach. We're not simply asking organisations whether they have plans, we are testing whether those plans are credible, connected across the whole system and capable of protecting safe care under pressure.

Our planning is informed by the 2026-27 winter respiratory modelling report, which covers scenarios in terms of flu, COVID-19, respiratory syncytial virus and combined infection scenarios. A supporting dashboard enables Welsh Government and NHS Wales to monitor national and local pressures and adapt the response as conditions change.

Our objective is clear: people should receive the right care in the right place without avoidable delay. More people should be supported to remain well at home. Those who need urgent, emergency or acute care should receive it quickly and safely, and nobody should remain in hospital longer than clinically necessary because support elsewhere is unavailable. Delivering that promise requires more than additional hospital capacity. Winter resilience depends on strong primary, community and social care services, rapid action when people become unwell, effective flow through hospitals and timely support for people to recover at home.

Diolch yn fawr iawn, Lywydd. Heddiw, dwi'n nodi'r camau pendant y mae'r Llywodraeth yma yn eu cymryd i amddiffyn pobl, cefnogi staff a chryfhau gwasanaethau iechyd a gofal ar draws Cymru y gaeaf hwn. Mi fydd y gaeaf yn heriol. Mi fydd y galw'n cynyddu, mi fydd salwch anadlol yn rhoi pwysau ychwanegol ar wasanaethau, ac mi fydd y cyfyngiadau o ran y gweithlu, cyllid a gofal cymdeithasol yn parhau i fod yn sylweddol.

Allwn ni ddim cael gwared ar bob risg, ond mi allwn ni baratoi'n gynharach, ymyrryd yn gyflymach a gofyn i bob rhan o'r system weithio gyda'i gilydd. Dyna pam rydyn ni wedi gweithredu'n gynt nag unrhyw Lywodraeth flaenorol yng Nghymru, gan ddangos arweinyddiaeth genedlaethol gryfach, disgwyliadau cliriach a ffocws di-baid ar gyflawni.

Mae pob bwrdd iechyd wedi cyflwyno fersiwn ddrafft o'u cynllun parodrwydd ar gyfer y gaeaf erbyn 1 Medi. Am y tro cyntaf, mae'r cynlluniau hynny'n cael eu profi'n drylwyr yn ystod mis Medi a mis Hydref fel bod risgiau, rhagdybiaethau a dibyniaethau yn cael eu herio, a chamau'n cael eu cymryd, cyn i'r pwysau gyrraedd y brig. Mae hyn yn cryfhau ein dull o weithredu yn sylweddol. Nid dim ond gofyn i sefydliadau a oes ganddyn nhw gynlluniau ydyn ni, rydyn ni'n profi a ydy'r cynlluniau hynny'n gredadwy, yn gweithio mewn ffordd gysylltiedig ar draws y system gyfan ac yn gallu sicrhau gofal diogel o dan bwysau.

Mae ein gwaith cynllunio'n cael ei lywio gan adroddiad modelu anadlol y gaeaf 2026-27, sy'n edrych ar senarios o ran y ffliw, COVID-19, firws syncytiol anadlol a chyfuniad o heintiau. Mae dangosfwrdd ategol yn galluogi Llywodraeth Cymru a NHS Cymru i fonitro pwysau cenedlaethol a lleol ac addasu'r ymateb wrth i'r amodau newid.

Mae ein nod yn glir: dylai pobl gael y gofal iawn yn y lle iawn heb oedi y gellir ei osgoi. Dylid cefnogi mwy o bobl i aros yn iach gartref. Dylai'r rhai sydd angen gofal brys, gofal mewn argyfwng neu ofal acíwt gael y gofal hwnnw yn gyflym ac yn ddiogel, a ddylai neb aros yn yr ysbyty yn hirach nag sy'n angenrheidiol yn glinigol oherwydd nad ydy cymorth ar gael mewn mannau eraill. Mae cyflawni'r addewid hwnnw yn gofyn am fwy na chapasiti ychwanegol mewn ysbytai. Mae gwydnwch y gaeaf yn dibynnu ar gael gwasanaethau sylfaenol, cymunedol a gofal cymdeithasol cryf, gweithredu'n gyflym pan fydd pobl yn mynd yn sâl, llif effeithiol drwy ysbytai a chefnogaeth amserol i bobl wella adref.

contributions.text_english:
That is why cross-cutting and cross-sector action is at the centre of our approach. Health boards, local authorities, ambulance services, primary care, housing, social care and voluntary organisations must plan and act as one system around the needs of individuals and communities. Community nursing, frailty services, single points of access, community response teams, hospital at home, rehabilitation and reablement all have a critical role. When these services work well, people are supported earlier, avoidable admissions are prevented and those leaving hospital can recover safely and independently at or close to home. This must include people who face the greatest barriers to care, including those experiencing homelessness, housing insecurity or social exclusion. Their needs don't fit neatly within organisational boundaries and neither should our response. This work is aligned with delivering health together and our ambition for an integrated community care system—a more sustainable model built on prevention, early intervention, community-based care and better integration.

For this winter, I'm setting three immediate priorities. First: protect people through vaccination, which continues to be the best safeguard against the transition of disease. Eligibility for the RSV vaccination has been expanded and health boards are working with Public Health Wales to improve the uptake of influenza vaccination among eligible people and staff. It is also vital that we continue to robustly counter at all times the dangerous anti-vax narratives pedalled by people who should know better.

Second: make every day count for patient flow. Health boards and local authorities are expected to apply 'home first', discharge to recover and assess, criteria-led discharge and trusted assessment consistently, seven days a week, so that people can leave hospital as soon as they are clinically ready.

Third: strengthen urgent care in the community. Single points of access, community response teams, hospital at home, same-day services and rapid clinical advice must help people receive earlier care and protect hospital capacity for those with the most urgent and complex needs. These aren't optional aspirations, they are delivery expectations. We'll monitor progress against clear operational evidence, including access to urgent care, ambulance handovers, hospital flow, discharge and community capacity. Where assurance is insufficient, organisations will be required to strengthen their response and take corrective action.

To support delivery, NHS Wales Performance and Improvement is making an additional £2 million available through the national urgent and emergency care improvement programme. It will be targeted at practical action before, during and after winter to improve acute hospital flow, accelerate safe discharge, reduce avoidable delay and strengthen patient safety at the points of greatest pressure. We'll expect health boards to demonstrate how that investment has improved delivery. A national winter planning session this month will bring together health boards' chief operating officers and local authority partners to resolve shared risks, reinforce joint accountability and maintain co-ordinated delivery throughout the winter.

Workforce availability remains a serious risk. Health boards must maintain safe, flexible and credible contingency arrangements, and national support will be targeted where it can make the greatest difference. But our responsibility goes beyond one winter. As a result of climate change, pressure no longer follows a predictable seasonal pattern. The record-breaking heatwaves of the summer months placed immense strains on our staff and estate alike, and it is essential that the lessons of adaptation from this year inform our approach to future years where hazardous heat levels will become the norm.

I'm therefore announcing that Wales will move to a comprehensive, continuous cycle of planning and preparedness, so that risks are assessed, learning is acted upon and resilience is strengthened throughout the year.

contributions.text_english:
The actions we are taking this winter are not separate from our wider ambitions for health and care in Wales. They are an early demonstration of the direction set out through 'delivering health together', our long-term ambition to improve outcomes, reduce inequalities and secure a sustainable health and care system for the future.

As set out in our programme for government, at the heart of our ambitions is a shift towards prevention, earlier intervention and more joined-up care. We cannot meet future demand through hospital care alone. We must do more to keep people healthy, support independence, intervene earlier when needs arise and provide more care in community settings. Achieving that ambition will require us to work closely with our partners across health, the social care sector and the wider public sector. In the immediate term, this means restoring grip where needed, improving performance and strengthening accountability.

At the same time, we must ensure that our workforce, our services, our digital infrastructure and our estates are equipped to meet the challenges of the future. Above all, we must pursue the longer term changes necessary to improve population health, reduce inequalities and shift our focus towards prevention, early intervention and care closer to home.

Llywydd, I want to conclude by thanking staff across hospitals, ambulance services, primary care, community teams, local authorities, care homes and voluntary organisations who are already preparing for the months ahead. Their professionalism and dedication are extraordinary. They deserve plans that are credible, decisions that are timely and leadership that is clear. This Government will provide that strong and proactive leadership. We will maintain rigorous national oversight, we'll work across Government and we'll act with partners to address risks and sustain improvement. We will judge success not by the quality of plans on paper, but by what people experience: safer and faster care, fewer avoidable delays, better support at home and services that remain resilient when pressure increases.

Our ambition is not simply to get through winter. It is, rather, to build a health and care system that is resilient, anticipates pressure, acts earlier, works as one and becomes stronger with every season. Thank you.

Dydy'r camau rydyn ni'n eu cymryd y gaeaf hwn ddim ar wahân i'n huchelgeisiau ehangach ar gyfer iechyd a gofal yng Nghymru. Maen nhw'n arwydd cynnar o’r cyfeiriad sy’n cael ei nodi drwy 'cyflawni iechyd gyda'n gilydd', ein huchelgais hirdymor i wella canlyniadau, lleihau anghydraddoldebau a sicrhau system iechyd a gofal gynaliadwy ar gyfer y dyfodol.

Fel y nodir yn ein rhaglen lywodraethu, yr hyn sydd wrth galon ein huchelgeisiau ydy newid i ganolbwyntio mwy ar atal, ymyrraeth gynharach a gofal mwy cydgysylltiedig. Allwn ni ddim cwrdd â'r galw yn y dyfodol drwy ofal mewn ysbytai yn unig. Mae'n rhaid inni wneud mwy i gadw pobl yn iach, cefnogi annibyniaeth, ymyrryd yn gynharach pan fydd anghenion yn codi a darparu mwy o ofal mewn lleoliadau cymunedol. Er mwyn cyflawni'r uchelgais honno, bydd angen inni weithio gyda phartneriaid ar draws y sector iechyd, y sector gofal cymdeithasol a’r sector cyhoeddus ehangach. Yn y tymor byr, mae hyn yn golygu adfer gafael lle bo angen, gwella perfformiad a chryfhau atebolrwydd.

Ar yr un pryd, mae’n rhaid inni wneud yn siŵr bod ein gweithlu, ein gwasanaethau, ein seilwaith digidol a’n hystadau mewn sefyllfa i allu cwrdd â heriau’r dyfodol. Yn fwy na dim, mae’n rhaid inni fynd ar drywydd y newidiadau hirdymor sydd eu hangen i wella iechyd y boblogaeth, lleihau anghydraddoldeb a symud ein ffocws tuag at atal, ymyrraeth gynnar a gofal yn agosach at y cartref.

Lywydd, dwi am gloi drwy ddiolch i’r holl staff mewn ysbytai, gwasanaethau ambiwlans, gofal sylfaenol, timau cymunedol, awdurdodau lleol, cartrefi gofal a sefydliadau gwirfoddol sydd eisoes yn paratoi ar gyfer y misoedd i ddod. Mae eu proffesiynoldeb a'u hymroddiad nhw yn anhygoel. Maen nhw'n haeddu cynlluniau sy'n gredadwy, penderfyniadau sy'n amserol ac arweinyddiaeth sy'n glir. Bydd y Llywodraeth hon yn darparu'r arweinyddiaeth gryf a rhagweithiol honno. Mi fyddwn ni'n sicrhau goruchwyliaeth genedlaethol drylwyr, yn gweithio ar draws y Llywodraeth, ac yn gweithio efo partneriaid i fynd i'r afael â risgiau a chynnal gwelliant. Mi fyddwn ni'n barnu llwyddiant nid yn ôl ansawdd y cynlluniau ar bapur, ond yn ôl yr hyn y mae pobl yn ei brofi: gofal mwy diogel a chyflymach, llai o oedi y gellir ei osgoi, gwell gefnogaeth gartref a gwasanaethau sy'n parhau i fod yn wydn pan fydd pwysau'n cynyddu.

Nid dim ond mynd drwy'r gaeaf ydy ein huchelgais ni. Ein huchelgais ni ydy adeiladu system iechyd a gofal sy'n wydn, yn rhagweld pwysau, yn gweithredu'n gynt, yn gweithio fel un ac yn cryfhau gyda phob tymor. Diolch.

contributions.text_english:
Thank you, Minister, for the advance notice of your statement today. I'd like to begin by associating myself with the comments you made about our NHS staff, who are the absolute backbone of the NHS in Wales, and they deserve a system that works for them and works effectively. I'm also glad that we're talking about winter preparedness today. Winter is something that has affected humanity every year since the dawn of time, and so it blows my mind that there still hasn't been proper planning in the Welsh NHS to deal with the pressures that we know are going to reoccur year after year.

However, I am slightly concerned about the current plans that are in place. Whilst doing research for the debate today, I came across this document. It's a self-assessment and assurance template that was published in the annex of the September board meeting notes from Swansea Bay University Health Board. In it, it outlines 90 key actions that the health board should undertake in order to begin preparing for winter. Of those 90, only 28 had been fully implemented, 61 had been partially implemented and one had not been implemented at all. This was something that was worrying to see to me, and I wonder, when it comes to these templates, what is the acceptable number of key actions that are completely implemented in order to be able to call this preparedness plan a success.

What are the enforcement mechanisms that are going to be used to ensure that health boards deliver here? You say, for example, that of your three priorities, they are not optional aspirations, they are delivery expectations, and that you would expect a health board to take corrective action and strengthen their response were they not to achieve them. But in this document, Swansea bay health board says that, when it comes to meeting the vaccination key actions, the significant risks to delivery are around limited capacity and lack of access to vaccination clinics.

Across all of the actions listed in that document, they say that eight key actions are at risk of full delivery due to insufficient workforce and seven key actions are at risk of delivery due to insufficient funding. Now, there is mention in your statement of £2 million being allocated as part of the urgent and emergency care improvement programme, but Audit Wales notes that the annual deficit for the NHS in 2025-26 was £199 million. So, if these health boards are already in deficit, and the only funding that has been made available clearly in your statement is £2 million, that seems to me like a drop in the ocean and not sufficient to implement these plans properly. So, are there any plans for additional resources to be allocated for winter preparedness? And if not, why not? If so, how many resources are going to be allocated and how much is that estimated to cost the taxpayer?

Now, something else that I found interesting about this document was to do with your comments about the plans needing to be tested in September and October of this year. Towards the end of the template, there is a self-assessment section and within it there are some local comments that have been made. It says this document has to be completed by a senior officer with sufficient oversight of the region's health and social care integrated plan to deliver the actions for winter 2026.

Now, in that self-assessment template, or the regional assurance template, rather, point 35 says that the plan should be tested during a winter exercise. The local comments in this document say, 'Which parts need testing? We don't have any resources for testing, and we only think that some bits are applicable for testing.' So, given that testing, you say, needs to occur within September and October, what is the progress of this testing? Has it all been completed already? And if it hasn't, do additional resources need to be allocated to our health boards in order to ensure that this testing can occur? And my suspicion is that the concerns are not just isolated to Swansea bay. I was able to see a screenshot of the same document from Powys Teaching Health Board in the annex of one of their recent board meeting documents. That screenshot showed that they would be unable to ensure pulmonary rehabilitation within two to four weeks after an exacerbation, because their current wait time for these services is between 20 and 36 weeks.

So, whilst I agree that we need to be focusing on winter preparedness, I'm personally concerned, given the evidence that I've seen today, about the health board's ability to implement on time. And I would like to ask you what your assessment is of the health board's ability to deliver these preparedness plans this winter and what actions are going to be taken to correct if they are not able to implement them. Diolch yn fawr.

contributions.text_english:
Thank you for those comments, and thanks for your opening remarks welcoming the fact that we have started the preparations earlier. In fact, I remember when I was asked to take this position, one of the first actions I did was ask for planning around winter preparedness, because, as you said right at the start of your contribution, this is something that happens annually, it's something that we should be prepared for. So, we've started earlier than ever before, which means that we are in a better position now than ever before to tackle the challenges that winter brings, and we know that those challenges and that winter is getting harder. I've also asked the NHS in Wales to look at the impact of the El Niño event as well, which is likely to have a significant detrimental impact on communities across Wales, and that needs to be taken into consideration.

But to your further points about the modelling and testing, yes, we are modelling those plans put forward by the health boards now. As I said, we're modelling them and testing them during September and October to see how robust they are. NHSPI is doing that work with the health boards, and, if we find weaknesses in the system, that gives us time then to correct course and find resolutions so that those weaknesses aren't highlighted when winter hits hard.

You asked about the limited capacity and the access to clinics with vaccination, for instance, and what other workforce or funding might be made available in the case of Swansea bay. As you said right at the beginning, this is an event that happens every year. So, this is part of their annual preparing. They should be budgeting for this. It's part of the budgets that they have and part of the work that they are preparing for year-round. So, I expect, the same as every other year, for them to deliver within budget. They're aware that this is happening. They are preparing for it.

And finally, you asked about the health board's need to prepare within the budgets and what assessment I've made of Swansea's plan. Now, I'm glad you finished right at the end there mentioning other health boards, because there's more than just Swansea in Wales. My assurance is moderate at the moment that they will be able to achieve the plans that they have set themselves—moderate currently, and we're just in early October now, based on the plans that I received in early September. Now that we're testing the plans that they've put forward—all the health boards and the trusts as well have put forward plans. We're testing them this month; we did a little bit last month. Having the learnings and the lessons from that testing, that assessment will increase over time, and I'm confident that we will be in a better position when winter comes and they will be in a better position to tackle the issues that winter brings to our communities.

Thank you for those comments, and thanks for your opening remarks welcoming the fact that we have started the preparations earlier. In fact, I remember when I was asked to take this position, one of the first actions I did was ask for planning around winter preparedness, because, as you said right at the start of your contribution, this is something that happens annually, it's something that we should be prepared for. So, we've started earlier than ever before, which means that we are in a better position now than ever before to tackle the challenges that winter brings, and we know that those challenges and that winter is getting harder. I've also asked the NHS in Wales to look at the impact of the El Niño event as well, which is likely to have a significant detrimental impact on communities across Wales, and that needs to be taken into consideration.

But to your further points about the modelling and testing, yes, we are modelling those plans put forward by the health boards now. As I said, we're modelling them and testing them during September and October to see how robust they are. NHSPI is doing that work with the health boards, and, if we find weaknesses in the system, that gives us time then to correct course and find resolutions so that those weaknesses aren't highlighted when winter hits hard.

You asked about the limited capacity and the access to clinics with vaccination, for instance, and what other workforce or funding might be made available in the case of Swansea bay. As you said right at the beginning, this is an event that happens every year. So, this is part of their annual preparing. They should be budgeting for this. It's part of the budgets that they have and part of the work that they are preparing for year-round. So, I expect, the same as every other year, for them to deliver within budget. They're aware that this is happening. They are preparing for it.

And finally, you asked about the health board's need to prepare within the budgets and what assessment I've made of Swansea's plan. Now, I'm glad you finished right at the end there mentioning other health boards, because there's more than just Swansea in Wales. My assurance is moderate at the moment that they will be able to achieve the plans that they have set themselves—moderate currently, and we're just in early October now, based on the plans that I received in early September. Now that we're testing the plans that they've put forward—all the health boards and the trusts as well have put forward plans. We're testing them this month; we did a little bit last month. Having the learnings and the lessons from that testing, that assessment will increase over time, and I'm confident that we will be in a better position when winter comes and they will be in a better position to tackle the issues that winter brings to our communities.

Can I thank you, Cabinet Minister, for your statement today? I am pleased that this is one of three statements on winter preparedness that Ministers are delivering today, and that recognises that planning for the winter months needs to be a cross-cutting approach.

In Government, of course, Welsh Labour began preparations for the winter months as early as possible, with preparations for last winter beginning in March 2025, with a winter summit for 2025-26. I am concerned that the actions taken by this Welsh Government mean the NHS isn't going into the winter in the robust shape that it needs to be. We still haven't heard from Ministers when two-year waits will be eliminated, just that it will be within a year, and that uncertainty certainly doesn't help the NHS or patients. After 10 months of waiting lists falling under the last Welsh Labour Government, they are now rising again under this Government. Ministers, of course, have been in dispute with health visitors in Cwm Taf, and now there's concern and uncertainty around the future of endometriosis services in Wales. All of this adds to the perception that the grip on health services is not firm enough as we go into the winter.

Minister, on the whole, this statement was light on detail and even lighter on financial commitments—more of a commentary than a detailed action plan for the winter. As you know, the extra £2 million that you referenced is a drop in the ocean for health budgets. Can you put a figure on the total actual resource that you are putting into winter pressures this year? Further to the questions that have been raised about stress testing of regional assessments, can you just outline what problems have so far been identified through that process and whether the problems that have been identified are now being addressed?

We know that, when hospitals come under pressure, the pressure on GP practices intensifies as well. The Royal College of General Practitioners have said that winter pressures for general practices are all too often overshadowed by the focus on acute hospital settings. So, what are you doing, Cabinet Minister, to ensure that GPs are properly supported going into the winter and what specific arrangements are you putting in place? Could you also give an update on how many more GPs have been recruited on your watch, given that we are now almost six months into the four-year term, during which the people of Wales are being promised 100 new and additional GPs?

Now, the programme for government also set out Ministers' intentions for greater use of evidence and data in the Welsh health service. So, can I ask you whether any targets have been put in place for winter preparedness, particularly around the uptake of vaccinations? I was very pleased that you called out dangerous misinformation about vaccinations. Could you just outline what additional effort is being made to provide facts on vaccinations to people who may be anxious about them? And more broadly, what is the Government doing to monitor and increase the take-up of vaccinations, especially for high-risk groups?

Now, in June, you said that the Government would be bringing forward proposals for a new communications approach that helps people get the right support and takes pressure off front-line services. Minister, I'd be very grateful if you could give an update on that new approach and whether it would be introduced in time for winter, and what key differences you anticipate it will make. Diolch.

Thank you for those questions. Llywydd, it's true that we've started earlier than ever before in planning for winter pressures. Now, the Member does point to other pressures within the health system: two-year waits, you've mentioned before, and I've responded to those issues numerous times, and we've made it clear that we will tackle those two-year waits. The money is now going into the system, with plans designed by clinicians and the health board, and we'll be seeing the result of that when we see the numbers coming through in the November period.

But those pressures, while they're there—. The winter pressures add further to the already current pressures that we've got in the NHS. That's why we are looking at frailty as an issue, making sure that we tackle frailty in the community. So, when you asked about GPs, it's making sure that GPs are supported in the community with district nurses so that we identify those issues earlier on, and, if frail patients do enter the front door of an A&E, that they're seen sooner, so that frailty is identified sooner, rather than people having to wait in the A&E for a longer time. So, that'll take pressure off the acute settings.

You asked about GP recruitment; you'll know that our target is to recruit an extra 100 GPs before the end of this Senedd term, which we will achieve when we reach that point. That will take pressure off in some communities where, currently, there's not enough resource in that primary care setting. So, that's a target that is clear; it's in our programme for government. 

And with vaccinations, currently, we've seen some improvement in the uptake of vaccinations in some of the most vulnerable parts of the community, especially in children, but it's very early, at this stage, to be able to monitor exactly if we're going to achieve an increase in the vaccination uptake. But, at the moment, it's looking promising. I am asking professionals in the health sector to make sure that they also take up the offer of a vaccination as well, because it's important in those acute settings especially, and with people who are mingling and working with people who are already ill, that they are vaccinated so that they don't share the illness when the time comes.

contributions.text_english:
Can I also thank the Cabinet Minister for his statement this afternoon? With winter looming, ensuring that the NHS is as prepared as can be for what might be lurking around the corner is indeed paramount. Winter is always a demanding time for our health service and hard-working staff, and, every year, winter brings additional pressures to our health service: more respiratory illness, more falls and fractures, more demand on emergency departments and more pressures on ambulances, and, inevitably, more pressure on staff.

Planning is essential, Cabinet Minister. We've all heard it, we all know it, but it's no good having a plan if we don't have the health service resilient enough to deliver it. That, in my view, boils down to capacity. I'd like to know: are you confident that we have a strong enough workforce to deal with the challenges that may crop up this winter? Are you confident that we have enough beds? And perhaps more importantly, are you confident that patients will be able to move through the system effectively? Cabinet Minister, back in July, you vowed to plan earlier for winter pressures—genuinely, a sensible move in my book. You promised a year-round approach to resilience, community care, better hospital flow and more of a focus on older people and those living with frailty. So, what has actually changed since July, because the figures still paint a worrying picture for me?

In August, the height of summer, nearly 1,400 patients across Wales were waiting longer than they should have to leave their hospital bed. This is up on the number of incidents of delayed transfers of care reported in the previous month. In total, these patients have been delayed for just shy of 60,000 days. So, if those were the figures in August, what will they be during the winter months, Cabinet Secretary? And what steps has the Government taken to ensure that those numbers start heading in the right direction, and when can we expect to see improvements? Cabinet Minister, are you confident that health boards and local authorities have the workforce and enough funding to prevent patients remaining in hospital unnecessarily this winter? What discussions have you had with health boards, local authorities and other key stakeholders to ensure the social care sector is on a strong footing to be able to ease the pressures?

Cabinet Minister, you say that winter preparedness plans submitted by health boards were being stress tested throughout September and into this month. Have major causes of concern been picked up at this stage? You talk about setting three immediate priorities for this winter, looking at vaccination, health boards and applying a home-first approach to discharge and strengthening urgent care in the community. Very noble claims, Cabinet Minister, but I have to agree with Ken Skates on this one—you've been very light on the detail in terms of how this is going to be achieved. [Interruption.] I know, I was shocked as well. So, an explanation on how this would be would be very much appreciated.

You said that £2 million is being allocated to health boards to help them improve acute hospital flow, accelerate safe discharge, reduce delay and strengthen patient safety. So, Cabinet Minister, are you confident that this funding is going to be enough? The Welsh Government quite rightly expects health boards to demonstrate how any extra funds have improved delivery, but what happens if they fail to do so? Previously, Cabinet Minister, you said the Government would reduce ambulance handover delays, tackle corridor care and shorten emergency department waits. But what are the specific targets for this winter, and what contingency action will be triggered if those targets are indeed missed? Because, Cabinet Minister, we still haven't seen enough progress in this area, and you cannot better prepare the NHS for winter pressures if it is already under immense strain as it is.

The Welsh Government has a target of ensuring that 95 per cent of patients should spend fewer than four hours in emergency departments. That target's never been met. According to the latest figures, only 63 per cent of patients spent under four hours in an A&E department in Wales during August. The Welsh Government has another target that no patient should wait longer than 12 hours in an emergency department. And guess what? That's never been hit either. Latest figures show that just under 11,000 people waited more than 12 hours in August this year.

Corridor care, as we all know, is a major problem in Wales, with the Royal College of Emergency Medicine previously finding that it was happening at all 12 emergency departments across Wales. Corridor care is dangerous and dehumanising, yet it's now common practice, and, frankly, Cabinet Minister, that's shameful. A report by Healthcare Inspectorate Wales released only last week declared that delayed patient handovers remain the most significant challenge facing the Welsh ambulance service, and that's before winter has even arrived. Clearly, it's not acceptable, so how can you expect people to believe things are going to be turning around in time for winter?

Prevention must be, therefore, at the heart of the winter strategy, and I welcome the Government's focus on vaccination, including the expansion of the RSV vaccine. We know that flu and other respiratory infections can indeed put significant pressures on the NHS, so every eligible person who takes up a vaccination is not only protecting themselves, they are helping to reduce avoidable pressures on our health and care services. In terms of an update, Cabinet Minister, we need to know whether vaccination programmes are reaching those most at risk. So, does the Welsh Government monitor this? Have any areas been identified where uptake is lagging? If so, what targeted action is taking place now? My final question, Cabinet Secretary, is simple: are you confident this Government and the health boards all across Wales are truly prepared for what is around the corner? Thank you.

contributions.text_english:
Llywydd, there were a number of questions there and a lot of statements as well. I agree with a number of the statements that you made. Regarding capacity, workforce, beds and flow, flow was a theme of your contribution, which I'll get on to in a minute, but, of course, the number of beds, whether we've got enough or not, is dependent on whether or not we can make sure that people don't enter that acute setting in the first place, tackling issues earlier on, which is why we are looking at that whole-system approach, making sure that we are shifting resources into the community, making sure that the primary care setting is resourced and has the support it needs in order to stop people from going there.

It would be remiss of me not to point out that community pharmacies play an important role here, especially with the common ailments scheme. Back in 2024-25, they gave 462,000 consultations. That's a massive amount of work that's done in our community pharmacies, and they play a crucial role also with vaccination as well. Getting those community-based services in place is crucial, and we're getting co-operation from those organisations, community pharmacies, GPs and others.

What's changed since July? Well, we've got plans now. The health boards have designed these plans, have presented them to us, we're testing them and making sure that we learn the lessons. So, we're going to be in a better position than ever before to face the pressures that inevitably will hit us when winter arrives.

You asked about the ambulances. Ambulance handovers are always a concern, and we need to see improvement in that space. We've seen some improvement over the last few months, which is a real positive, and we need to see that sustained over the coming few months, because as you say, winter is going to present a different challenge, but I am glad that we're seeing those improvements in the ambulance service.

Finally, you mentioned social services, and I'm really glad that you did. It's forgotten far too often in the discussions around the impact on the health service, but more importantly on individuals. And, yes, the social care sector, social services, are crucial in this. We're making sure that the COOs, the chief operating officers of health boards, are meeting up with leaders of social services in local authorities to develop that plan, making sure that they're aligned and that we can have improved discharges.

We're looking at improved patient flow—which is the theme, as I said, you looked at in your contribution—and the transition home, starting the planning for the discharge process earlier, making sure that we've got a seven-day approach to that, with expected discharge dates and regular senior clinical reviews of those discharges, so that people can go home sooner than they are currently doing.

contributions.text_english: We start with Elyn Stephens.
contributions.text_original: Rydym ni'n dechrau gyda Elyn Stephens.

contributions.text_english:
Diolch, Lywydd. Gweinidog Cabinet, winter pressures are often discussed in terms of hospital capacity, delayed discharges and access to primary care, but in the communities that I represent, there's also the very basic issue of whether people can physically get to hospital at all. Living in the shadow of the Rhigos mountain, I know personally how dependent communities in Afan Ogwr Rhondda are on mountain roads, such as the Rhigos, the Bwlch—Bwlch y Clawdd to friends—and Maerdy mountain.

These are essential routes for people getting to hospital and for ambulance crews getting patients to urgent and emergency care. During periods of snow and ice, those roads can close very quickly with little communication, leaving communities effectively cut off. What assurances can the Cabinet Secretary give that winter preparedness plans include specific contingencies for mountain road closures, including joint working between health boards, the ambulance services and local authorities, so that patients in those communities are not left without safe access to care?

contributions.text_english:
Absolutely, people will want assurances and to understand that the ambulance will arrive on time. I don't know how many of you saw the film Effi o Blaenau, which showed how an ambulance during winter didn't arrive on time and the cataclysmic consequences of that. Now, we're not in that position; that was a film. But, yes, people will want to be assured that those ambulances can reach them. And, yes, we've got four local resilience forums operating along the police boundaries here in Wales, and they ensure that the emergency services, the NHS and local authorities develop those contingency plans in the event of road closures or catastrophic incidents around the weather.

So, they'll have control and grip on that, which makes sure that ambulances will be able to find and reach their destination. The Welsh Ambulance Services University NHS Trust is also preparing for what we call the predictable winter risks, especially for rural mountainous areas, including severe weather and the pressures that rural areas provide. So, WAST is preparing for that, and people can be assured that they will be there.

contributions.text_english: Thank you very much for your statement, Minister, and I note this follows a statement you made on 1 July, when temperatures were slightly warmer than they are now. I'm very pleased as well that, in your statement, you refer to those vulnerable groups, particularly people who are homeless. And I just really wanted to just focus on this, because for those people who are homeless in winter, it literally is about getting a home. That will save their lives. Crisis in Wales reported, this month, that 63 people died on the streets in 2025 in Wales. The average age of a woman dying, who is homeless, was 43, and 47 for men. Crisis says it's preparing for a busy winter. They want the UK Government to unfreeze the housing benefit, but it does call on the Welsh Government to enact the new Homelessness and Social Housing Allocation (Wales) Act 2026. So, what will you be doing to work across the Government, but also to support those third sector organisations, such as Crisis, to get homeless people literally off our streets this winter? Diolch yn fawr iawn, Lywydd.

Year after year, the previous Government failed to prepare sufficiently for the winter months. In May, the people of Wales put their faith in this Plaid Cymru Government to prioritise our NHS. And I welcome the statement today, which is breaking the cycle of waiting for winter to arrive before reaching it.

Many of the priorities set out in the statement can only succeed through local implementation. Could the Cabinet Minister please provide more detail on how the Government will support those providing healthcare in our communities? They are often under-resourced and under immense pressure, but if we can get this right, it would reduce the pressure on A&E, keeping people in their communities and out of hospital, where there is a chance they would pick up further illness and infection. Diolch.

contributions.text_english: Llywydd, I agree with the Member that those providing healthcare in our communities are under significant pressure. And again, let's recognise the work that nurses, community nurses, GPs, allied health professionals and others do in this field. We owe a debt of gratitude to them. We know that pressures in our emergency departments are often a symptom of the pressures elsewhere in the system, which is why we've set in place a programme to shift resources into the community, making sure that primary care is properly resourced. We've got the Community by Design transformation programme, ensuring that we have a community and home first approach. District nursing, for instance, remains at the heart of the approach that we're taking. Across Wales, there are 167 neighbourhood district nursing teams providing a 24/7 service, and undertaking more than 230,000 visits every month. So, that's the work that we've got in place; that's why we're making sure, and how we're making sure, that people are seen closer to home. If we are to make sure that the acute settings are protected, that hospital spaces and intensive care units are protected, then we have to make sure that we've got those services in the community, treating people at home.

Cabinet Minister, when ice and snow arrive, disabled people are often the first to be cut off from healthcare. A wheelchair user cannot safely cross an untreated pavement, and someone who relies on accessible transport may find services cancelled without notice. Missed appointments can mean delayed treatment, and too often, a crisis that ends in hospital.

Cabinet Minister, what guidance has been given to the health boards to make sure that disabled patients are offered flexible alternatives, such as home visits, rescheduling without penalty, or remote consultations where appropriate, when severe weather prevents them from travelling? And how will health boards work with local authorities and transport providers, so that routes to key health sites remain accessible throughout the winter? Diolch.

Diolch, Lywydd. I thank the Cabinet Minister for your statement today. Can I join you in thanking all those NHS staff across the country doing a lot of work under extreme circumstances? Now that I've stepped back from the shadow health role, and I'm sitting a little bit closer to the exit, I just want to remind you, and just reassure you, really, that it's no reflection on my job of scrutinising you over the NHS performance here in Wales. Because, Cabinet Minister, in opposition, you criticised Labour's winter plans as 'short-term sticking plasters' and 'no solutions' and challenged the absence of clear targets. Today, you said your Government has acted 'earlier than ever before', with health boards' plans being stress-tested and an additional £2 million for urgent and emergency care.

And will you today—because I know you do like targets, Cabinet Minister—publish measurable targets, reducing ambulance handover delays, emergency department waiting times, and delayed discharges, so that we can actually judge whether your Government's plans are actually delivering, and worth the paper they're written on?

contributions.text_english: Today, I am providing an update on the resilience of Wales's transport network and the action that is being taken by the Welsh Government, Transport for Wales and our partners in order to prepare for a changing climate. Reducing carbon emissions remains very important to us. But, in addition to that, we need to prepare for the impacts of climate change, which are already being felt by communities across Wales. People rightly expect transport services to be there when they need them. That is why making sure that our network is reliable and ready to cope with extreme events is such an important responsibility.

The weather conditions—[Interruption.] Diolch. I appreciate that. The weather conditions experienced across Wales this year have demonstrated how rapidly climate risks are changing. Wales has faced prolonged rainfall, drought, extreme heat and significant wildfire incidents. These are not simply environmental issues, they are transport issues too. These events have reinforced the need to adapt our transport networks so that they can continue to operate safely and reliably in a changing climate.

Later this month, the First Minister will convene a wildfire summit, bringing together the public and private sectors and trade unions to identify ways to reduce the risk of wildfires and make sure we are better prepared to respond when they occur. Extreme heat and wildfires have placed exceptional pressure on infrastructure, services, passengers and staff. I recognise the work of transport organisations, emergency services, local authorities, trade unions and other partners in maintaining safe travel and protecting critical links.

Through my engagement with operators and trade unions, I have heard first-hand the impact that extreme heat, wildfire risk and other severe weather events can have on front-line staff. Their safety and well-being must come first. We will work with Transport for Wales and trade unions to make sure the experience of front-line workers informs the practical measures we put in place. Transport employers must plan for these risks, working with trade unions to identify measures that protect staff and support the safe operation of services.

The challenges experienced across the network this summer demonstrated why this preparation is increasingly important. On the rail network, high temperatures required some trains to be withdrawn because of cooling-system problems. Infrastructure operated close to—and, at times, beyond—historic design limits, leading to speed restrictions and additional failures. But this is not just a rail issue.

Although the most visible impacts this summer were on rail, resilience matters across every mode. Extreme temperatures affected bus services, while flooding, landslips and heat are placing growing pressure on roads and active travel infrastructure. The same principle applies to the international gateways on which Wales depends for connectivity, trade and economic activity.

Our major ferry ports—Holyhead, Fishguard and Pembroke Dock—provide vital international connections for people and goods. The prolonged disruption at Holyhead in December 2024 demonstrated how important our ports are to communities, businesses and the wider Welsh economy. It also showed how quickly disruption at one strategic gateway can have wider consequences. The Irish sea taskforce was established in response, to consider how a similar incident could be avoided and how partners should respond if one occurred at any Welsh port. I intend to publish a six-month update on its recommendations this autumn.

Investment is also strengthening port resilience. Stena Line has committed significant investment in infrastructure at Holyhead and Fishguard to improve resilience, connectivity and future capacity. During my recent visit to Ireland, I met Minister Canney and key stakeholders to discuss resilience and co-operation across these vital routes. I have also asked officials to prepare a joint exercise based on the scenario of an unforeseen Welsh port closure.

These lessons about preparedness, co-ordination and contingency planning apply to other strategic gateways. Cardiff Airport maintains emergency planning arrangements for incidents including severe weather and winter storms. Across aviation and ports, preparedness depends on clear responsibilities, tested plans, and effective communication. Strong partnerships are equally important across the wider network. My officials have established the Wales transport adaptation working group, bringing together infrastructure managers, operators and key stakeholders to support a co-ordinated approach.

I have asked Transport for Wales to take immediate steps to improve resilience to weather conditions that can no longer be treated as exceptional. In the short term, this includes strengthening maintenance and inspection regimes, working to improve the reliability of train cooling systems and taking practical measures to reduce heat impacts on rolling stock. Enhanced weather monitoring, clearer escalation arrangements and pre-planned operational responses will improve preparedness and help reduce disruption during periods of severe weather. The aim is simple: to act earlier, reduce disruption and keep people moving safely.

Alongside these immediate measures, Transport for Wales is developing a longer term adaptation programme. This will embed resilience in the way transport services are planned, operated and invested in for the future. Transport for Wales will work closely with Network Rail, which operates much of the rail infrastructure in Wales, so that plans cover the whole network. Priorities will include better climate-risk information, stronger drainage and earthworks, resilient rail and bus specifications, new monitoring technology, and nature-based solutions. The work will also support the wider cross-Government approach to climate adaptation and resilience that will be reflected through the forthcoming climate and nature action plan.

On the strategic road network, lessons from recent storms, floods and heatwaves are shaping how we manage and maintain our roads, helping us become better prepared for future disruption. We're also working with local authorities to strengthen the wider highway network and rolling out resilience and adaptation training across all 22 authorities. As we move into winter, preparations reflect the growing risks of heavy rainfall, flooding, landslips, storms and coastal impacts, alongside projections for warmer, wetter winters and more intense rainfall. The central lesson is clear: resilience is not simply about maintaining assets; it is about enabling people to travel safely and reliably.

We cannot limit ourselves to responding to today's incidents. We must prepare for the climate of the decades ahead while continuing to reduce emissions. Working with our partners, the Welsh Government is taking practical actions to build a transport system that can withstand future pressures and continue to serve the people of Wales. We cannot prevent every disruption caused by extreme weather, but we can be better prepared, more resilient and more responsive. We can identify risks earlier, act faster when disruption happens, and make sure our network is built and maintained to withstand the conditions we know are coming.

Transport for Wales will work closely with Network Rail, which operates much of the rail infrastructure in Wales, so that plans cover the whole network. Priorities will include better climate-risk information, stronger drainage and earthworks, resilient rail and bus specifications, new monitoring technology, and nature-based solutions. The work will also support the wider cross-Government approach to climate adaptation and resilience that will be reflected through the forthcoming climate and nature action plan.

On the strategic road network, lessons from recent storms, floods and heatwaves are shaping how we manage and maintain our roads, helping us become better prepared for future disruption. We're also working with local authorities to strengthen the wider highway network and rolling out resilience and adaptation training across all 22 authorities. As we move into winter, preparations reflect the growing risks of heavy rainfall, flooding, landslips, storms and coastal impacts, alongside projections for warmer, wetter winters and more intense rainfall. The central lesson is clear: resilience is not simply about maintaining assets; it is about enabling people to travel safely and reliably.

We cannot limit ourselves to responding to today's incidents. We must prepare for the climate of the decades ahead while continuing to reduce emissions. Working with our partners, the Welsh Government is taking practical actions to build a transport system that can withstand future pressures and continue to serve the people of Wales. We cannot prevent every disruption caused by extreme weather, but we can be better prepared, more resilient and more responsive. We can identify risks earlier, act faster when disruption happens, and make sure our network is built and maintained to withstand the conditions we know are coming.

Minister, I've listened very carefully to the statement, and I remain concerned that we are hearing far more about the challenges facing our transport network than the actual action being taken to address them. The reality is that passengers across Wales have been putting up with an unreliable railway for far too long. Last year, Transport for Wales was amongst the worst-performing rail operators in Britain for cancellations. Passengers are paying substantial fares for services that are too often delayed, disrupted or cancelled altogether.

Whilst extreme weather presents a genuine challenge, as it does every single year, it can't become a convenient explanation for every failure. The Government is responsible for ensuring our transport network is fit for purpose, whatever the season. So, Minister, what specific improvements are being made to the reliability of services, particularly across the core Valleys lines, and when can passengers expect to see those benefits?

I'd also like to raise the serious issue of air conditioning on our trains. Since April, there have been approximately 1,000 reported air conditioning faults, with 350 recorded in June alone. Those figures are unacceptable for a modern railway. We cannot expect passengers to travel in excessive heat, nor should we expect drivers, conductors and other railway staff to work in those conditions. I would therefore welcome confirmation of what action has been agreed with Transport for Wales, what timetables have been established and how staff and passenger safety will be protected.

Minister, if I could turn to flooding now, communities such as Pontypridd have experienced repeated devastating disruption, and I pay tribute to constituency Members across all parties for their work on this. We have seen roads closed, rail services suspended and businesses affected, sometimes for considerable periods. Yet there's very little in today's statement about the funding being made available to protect those vulnerable routes. What additional investment is being committed, and what practical measures are being taken alongside the Minister responsible for flood prevention?

I also want to address the resilience of our ports and the strategic roads serving them. Holyhead, Fishguard and Pembroke are essential to the Welsh economy and our trading relationship with Ireland. The closure of Holyhead in December 2024 demonstrated how vulnerable those connections can be. The A55 Menai crossings, the A40 and the A477 are vital routes for businesses, freight operators and communities that depend on them. Any prolonged disruption has serious economic consequences. Your Irish sea taskforce has already recognised these concerns, and an update has already been promised this autumn. So, Minister, can you confirm if that update will include firm commitments, allocated funding and delivery dates, or are we facing another round of recommendations without any certainty of action?

Minister, I recognise that protecting our transport infrastructure against extreme weather is not straightforward. Plaid has had years in opposition to identify these problems and develop solutions hand-in-hand with your bedfellows of Labour. The issue is no longer whether the Government understands those problems—it's whether it has the determination to resolve them. Passengers need reliable trains, businesses need dependable roads, and communities need proper protection against flooding. These are not unreasonable expectations. They are the basic responsibilities of Government. After years of promises, reviews and strategies, the people of Wales are entitled to expect something more substantial. They are entitled to see results. Diolch.

I'm really pleased that Reform is starting to recognise that the climate is starting to cause us real problems on our transport network, because, ultimately, what we're dealing with is the result of years of not addressing the climate issues carefully and properly.

On railways, Transport for Wales I think have managed to see the last—. We had five heatwaves, as we all know, during the summer, and those caused a huge amount of pressure on the Transport for Wales operations. What we noticed is that each time those operations were affected, the resilience was better, because it's not just about dealing with the consequences of that particular action, it's about making sure you improve, and that they improve time and time again. On your point about their service delivery, they've just appeared top of the tree when it comes to services in the most recent period, and I think that bears testament to the work that they're doing, particularly on the core Valleys lines.

Specific improvements related to air conditioning—I think that's a really good point. The air conditioning needs to work for passengers and needs to work for the people who are working on the trains as well. We're carrying on with the investment in the rolling stock to make sure we've got the trains that are suitable for the future. We've still got old stock on our railways. They're going to be taken off those railways as we move forward. But a point that I made a few weeks ago in the Siambr about us being responsible for all of our rail network would enable us to do these things quicker, which at the moment your party doesn't support. I too was next to the Minister for rural resilience talking about flooding earlier, and I think the issues—. He made reference to transport, and I was going to make reference to the work that he's got going on, because this is a Government that's working hand in glove across our portfolios to make sure we support each other.

One of the last points in my statement was that we can't stop every major incident from happening when it comes to the weather. These weather conditions are—. The new normal is quite different to what the old past was and it's catching up with us very quickly. But the point about being able to adapt very quickly and prepare ourselves for these issues is critical. And also I think that one of the things that particularly passengers want is that they want to know when things are going to happen. Making sure that we keep people informed is of critical importance.

I'm glad you mentioned ports, because I've spent a lot of time in ports over recent months, and I too recognise the importance that they play. When I went to Ireland, what I found striking was the importance that Holyhead played to the Irish economy and therefore to the European economy of getting goods into Wales and through to the rest of the UK. Holyhead is the second biggest roll-on, roll-off port in the country. What we've seen is that the investment that's been made since the December 2024 report is about to come online. My key concern, though, is that the weather conditions will be as dangerous and we could see as many problems this winter as we've seen in previous winters, which is the reason that I've set a piece of work off that will test what we would do in these circumstances, because the last time this happened, it was very, very close to Christmas and people had to make decisions without having been through this before. So, this is about being clear about whose responsibilities are there and also the responsibilities of UK Government in this. Only UK Government can redirect ships. That's not my responsibility. So, working with them in this is absolutely key. I look forward to outlining the Irish sea taskforce recommendations. There will be firm recommendations out of there, and I hope to get cross-Siambr support for those recommendations because they talk directly to the resilience issues that you brought up.

The final point that I just want to make—. You talked about roads. This is one of the things that I think is of most concern, and this comes back to the point I made in my Menai and M4 contributions a week ago. We need to make sure we invest in our strategic road network, because it's been underinvested in in the past. Taking care of our core assets is the key way of making sure we can maintain the resilience we've got now. So, that's a central plank of the announcement I made last week and it's something I'm focused on going forward.

Thank you, Deputy Minister, for your statement here this afternoon. Climate change is an ever-growing challenge for our transport network. Extreme weather leading to flooding, landslips and wildfires are leading to ever greater disruption. And we know this winter is likely to be worse than those in previous years due to the El Niño weather system aggravating the rapidly growing impact of climate change.

So, all parties in this Siambr should welcome your work, Deputy Minister, in seeking to enhance preparedness and reduce disruption to everyday life and economic activity from the potential for extreme weather to force the closure of our transport networks. I particularly welcome the proposed joint exercises with the Irish Government and ferry operators with regard to maintaining access to ferry ports following events at Holyhead port last year.

Deputy Minister, you are clearly leading a focused response within Welsh Government and Transport for Wales to reduce transport disruption this winter, with that focus on rail and trunk roads. However, I do have some concerns that maybe not enough is being done to protect the whole system. Most roads are owned and maintained by local government, and in my own constituency, both Merthyr Tydfil County Borough Council and Rhondda Cynon Taf County Borough Council are working hard to clear drains and gullies to improve the resilience of the local road network in advance of those winter months.

So, what actions are you taking, Deputy Minister, to ensure that local authorities have the resources they need to enable those local responses to climate adaptation? How much new money is the Government going to make available to improve road maintenance by local government, including drainage works to reduce the incidence of flooding on local authority roads?

Rail and roads get a good mention in your statement, Deputy Minister, however we know the most used mode of public transport is bus services. So, what actions are you taking to include the bus industry in climate adaptation and resilience planning? I think this is particularly important in light of Transport for Wales taking ownership of a franchised bus system.

I am a little concerned, maybe, Minister, that you might be taking a bit of a supplier-orientated approach to climate adaptation and resilience. So, what will you do to improve information for communities, councils and travellers by rail, car, bus and active travel about the general challenges that we face from transport disruption, and more urgently to support the improvement of communication and information flows for communities and travellers who may be in the throes of a severe weather event?

Over the summer, I visited a farm in my constituency that is farmed by the members of the Nature Friendly Farming Network and they highlighted a range of environmental improvements to their farm, some of which were delivered under the sustainable farming scheme, which I know some environmental groups are concerned that maybe this Welsh Government won't continue. They told me something quite interesting relating to transport. There's a major railway line at the bottom of their farmland that had been quite badly affected by seasonal flooding over the years, but since they carried out a range of interventions, including tree and hedge planting, those incidents had really declined, improving the resilience of the railway network. It's something that I mentioned during the rural resilience Minister's statement earlier, but what discussions have you had across Government with him, and others maybe, about how nature-based solutions such as these could be used to reduce the impact on our travel network?

Ultimately, however, the effectiveness of climate adaptation and resilience interventions will depend on budgetary provision. So, what new money will you, Deputy Minister, be investing in climate adaptation and resilience across the transport system in the financial year to March 2027 and next year in 2027-28? In short, Minister, are you prepared to put your money where your mouth is?

And thank you for the general support for this statement as well. I think this is the work—. This summer has been a remarkable summer. Things have changed, and I think even most people who were previously sceptical of climate change have seen the impacts of it all around us. I think people are seeing it in their day-to-day lives. Sometimes late to the party, lots of people, but, ultimately, that's been important.

I think your point about the whole-system approach is really important. We've got the regional transport funds as well that have started on their process at the moment. Part of that is about making sure that they build resilience into their funding bids. I'll just reflect on Elyn Stephens's point in the last debate about getting over the Bwlch to get into the hospitals, and these are real issues that are part of this whole resilience package.

Now, the strategic road networks aren't in those such vulnerable positions as some of the roads that are in the control of the local authorities. So, there is partnership working between the local authorities. I referenced it in my statement, and that's been heightened by the fact that the need to be able to solve things, whether it's education or health, is really critical to this. So, I'm looking for much improved regional transport plans that look at the strategic impact of making sure our roads are accessible over winter and summer, because the strategic road network is impacted by heat waves as well as by winter. Winter seems more acute, especially as we're going into it now.

I'm really pleased you mentioned bus. I did reference bus in the statement, but bus is the key way that people get across our country via public transport. It's used by many more people than the rail service is and it's often, at times, forgotten. Buses were affected in this heat wave this summer. There were bus services that were drawn from operation because they were too hot for the driver to operate and also for the passengers in there as well. And I think the lessons learned from this are actually about moving ahead.

You've mentioned bus franchising. A part of that is about a bus renewal plan, so the new fleet we need, the fleets for the future, and we've got lots of those. You've seen them. If you're around our capital city, you will have seen electric buses that have got air conditioning. They work really well. And we've got other places around Wales that are still using diesel buses without air conditioning. So, there is a plan to move all buses into that. But there's also some simple stuff we can do. When we paint a roof of a bus white instead of black, it makes a real difference. The Taith Cymru coaches, which we're launching in two weeks' time, have all got white roofs. White roofs take about 4 degrees out of the temperature of the cab. Now, that cab is air conditioned, but the fact you can therefore make the whole system work better and the engines work better without having to cool the cab is really important. So, there's some really simple stuff we can do as well.

I apologise if I didn't say enough about the passenger. I think the passenger is central to this and I mentioned it in my answer to Jason a few minutes ago as well. Part of this is about being clear about our communication. There will be things that we can't address. There will be services that will have to stop where it's unsafe, because safety is the critical thing. But I think one of the things that we're getting a lot better at is understanding the forecasts that come in, preparing for them and being able to inform customers. Because part of what we all, I think, want is an integrated transport system. So, it's all very well if you can catch the bus to the train station, but if the train's not running, what's the point of catching the bus? So, I think that integration of message is absolutely key.

Your last point about joined-up thinking, and especially linking into other things that are going on—. The farmers who are doing some work that positively impacts the rail network underneath—I referenced the climate and nature action plan. That isn't my responsibility, it's a cross-Government responsibility. So, feeding into that can make a real difference, and a tangible difference to our rail and other transport infrastructure as well. So, it's a really good point. Diolch yn fawr iawn.

Thanks for your statement. [Laughter.] Now, as someone who uses the train service in particular—I'll mention buses in a minute—this summer in particular highlighted to me just how we always tend to think it's the winter, with the leaves and everything on the line and the bad weather, where disruptions come, but we've faced it all in terms of the transport network here. Extreme weather is becoming a more frequent occurrence, and nobody in this Chamber can deny that. 

We're already seeing the consequences of inadequate planning across our transport system. Direct train services between Pontypridd and Cardiff Bay have been cancelled for a prolonged period, because more trains than usual are requiring repairs. And I think it's the 137s. Those trains are just—. In this day and age, I can't, for the life of me, imagine why we put a load of trains on a line whereby if the air conditioning in summer packs up, there are no windows, so, basically, it's very, very uncomfortable, and I would just say that the thinking behind that just baffles me.

In north Wales, we're also facing significant disruption, and I think Mair mentioned it earlier. I am dreading January to 6 February next year, with rail replacement buses being provided. Because, quite often, when I get on a train to come down here, I don't know whether it's going to be a four-hour journey or a five-hour journey. I've even had a seven-hour journey on more than one occasion down here. So, how you're going to make sure that, not just for us as Members, but anybody using the rail service and then having to rely on buses—.
