My biggest bone of contention when I'm on a train is, sure enough, we have to get up and we have to change to another train, but the lack of information is just—it's unbelievable. You get told different stories by the conductor. I then have been known to contact Transport for Wales myself directly and you get told something completely different. And I remember a time when Tom Montgomery had to wait several hours—. I was lucky because somebody came to give me a lift, but I think he had about nine hours to get from north Wales down here.

Now, these closures are going to place already enormous pressure on other transport services and cause considerable stress. Points have been made about people with disabilities, older passengers and those with limited transport alternatives. Disruption can create additional barriers to accessing essential services. These pressures are not confined to particular routes or specific times of the year; they do reflect wider challenges. Jason mentioned the reputation that Transport for Wales has, and I've done a survey today and I make no apology for, when responding, saying, 'Poor, poor, poor'. I'm sorry but the facts speak for themselves: 14,272 trains were cancelled in Wales throughout 2025; 880 cancellations were attributed to points failures. Another thing, Cabinet Minister, is that I'm told in letters by James Price, 'We don't have a points problem in Wales'; I'm sorry, but you do, because, quite often, signalling and points failures put lots of extra time onto our journeys. So, whatever needs to be done, sort the points and the signal failures out. Driver-related issues—this surprised me—were responsible for 843 cancellations. There must be other Members here who've got to a station only to be told, 'We're waiting for the driver; we haven't got a driver.' In this day and age, I can't understand why we end up in those situations. Severe flooding, of course, caused 250 cancellations. But it just demonstrates the scale of disruption that passengers experience and it does raise important questions about how effectively our transport network is being maintained and prepared for the future. Every cancellation represents more than a statistic. It can mean a missed medical appointment. I was sat with a young man who was deeply stressed because he had an interview to go to and, whilst he was there, he actually had the job turned down because he couldn't get to his appointment on time.

You don't need me, Minister—and I've run out of time anyway—to tell you all the problems that—. I could speak for an hour on this alone, but I'm not going to, I won't be allowed—

Diolch, Janet. I always welcome your contributions. I think that, in all seriousness, your real-life experience—. I remember when you and Tom were stuck and Tom—. So, these things do happen. I think that the interesting thing, for the purposes of this, is that we're talking about how we can manage better with issues of, particularly, extreme weather. But I think your points about the fact that, sometimes, other issues exacerbate some of those problems is worth noting into it as well.

I think we do have your support for the devolution of rail, but you mentioned the point about—[Interruption.] We'll try. You mentioned the point about points failures, and these are Network Rail's points, in the main, especially the routes that you're taking. So, the responsibility for those railways is being managed elsewhere. Now, I'm not denigrating the fact that they're working hard to do some of these things, but we're not the priority in some of these changes. So, I think one of the things that this talks to is the fact that we want to take responsibility for us. And the improvement in the services on the core Valleys lines—when we've got the whole service; we've got the track, the train and everything else—is marked and it's been marked and it's improving month on month. I think that talks to what sort of rail system we could have in the future. I'm really pleased that you talked about how disruption affects the most vulnerable first, and I think that's, again, something that links back to the conversation with Vikki and with Jason about making sure that our communication is really clear, particularly to those people who may not be able to find that the journey—. It's already a challenge, the journey that we've got. And part of that, I think, talks to us about making sure that we communicate in a way that's most effective for the people who are taking the journey as well—that's really critical for it.

I just think the last—. Just in terms of passengers requiring accurate information, I think that that is also something that—. I feel that this young guy who you were talking to who missed his job appointment as well, some of that is about—. And again, I'm linking it to how do we make sure that, particularly in extreme weather conditions, we get these things right so that communications are clear as we go through.

The last point: at the start of this I made a commitment to make a statement on the north Wales main line changes, that was obviously a Network Rail decision to close that main line. The communication around that initially was really poor—we found out by accident rather than by design. But, because we found out early enough, we can get in there and make sure that we've got these bus replacement services that do their best to be able to pick up the slack. Now this isn't the way that you'd want to go and plan it, because everyone in the north of the country now must be dreading what's going to happen in January, including Members in this room as well, so I understand that. What I can do, as transport Minister, is make sure that, where we've got those rail replacement services, they run regularly, they're good services, they're also services that can hit the timetables that we were hitting before. So, hopefully, disruption will be kept to a minimum, because we've got a bit more time to plan for this than we should have had. But, ultimately, this was a decision that was made without our say-so, and it was made to us, not with us.

Diolch, Lywydd. Over the last few months, as Wales experienced its hottest summer on record, it became hard to deny that extreme climate conditions are, sadly, becoming our new normal. As a result, many of us will be looking to make more sustainable choices in the hopes of helping to minimise the devastating effects of climate change.

One change I would encourage everyone to make is to prioritise using public transport over cars wherever possible. Taking a train instead of a car for medium-length distances can reduce journey emissions by 80 per cent. It seems like an obvious choice. However, access to public transport itself can be limited by climate change. We have all seen snowfall, heat or high winds bring transport services to a standstill.

How will the Minister ensure that, while we continue to build a more resilient transport infrastructure, all forms of public transport in Wales are effectively connected so that, even in adverse conditions, there's always an option available to those who wish to use it?

Diolch. So, I think this is a choice—. There's no choice between decarbonisation and adaptation. I think these things need to run hand in hand. But for us to provide a solution that works for people, the public transport system must work. That's the reason I'm really keen to make sure bus franchising works and gets on and that we get that in the timetable that we've suggested, because that's about connecting people in the way they want to travel.

Footpaths are an essential, but often overlooked part of the transport network across Wales. Well-maintained pavements and footpaths are particularly important for older people, people with mobility difficulties, wheelchair users, people with prams or pushchairs, as well as the 20 per cent of Welsh households without a car. 

As we've heard this afternoon, poor winter weather will soon be with us. Flooding and icy nights will inevitably speed up the degradation of our footpaths. Accidents caused by uneven paving slabs and hidden hazards within deceptively deep puddles lead to pressure on NHS services, or to people feeling just too scared to go out.

Maintenance of footpaths is the responsibility, of course, of local authorities, but what will the Minister be doing to support them to keep paths in good condition this winter, as well as make proactive adaptions to prevent future damage in extreme weather events and keep them open and accessible for everyone who needs them?

Thank you very much, Dirprwy Lywydd, and I move the motion to approve the Child Minding and Day Care Exceptions (Revocation and Transitional Provision) (Wales) (Amendment) Order 2026. This is a short and technical amending instrument that is required to keep the statute book clear, accurate and consistent. The Child Minding and Day Care Exceptions (Revocation and Transitional Provision) (Wales) (Amendment) Order 2026 will replace the Child Minding and Day Care Exceptions (Wales) Order 2010 from 1 April 2027.

As a consequence of the revoking and replacing of the 2010 exceptions Order with the 2026 exceptions Order, references to the 2010 exceptions Order in existing legislation must be updated. This amendment Order makes these necessary changes. This amendment Order replaces relevant references to the 2010 exceptions Order on the statute book with references to the 2026 exceptions Order.

This amendment Order does not alter the policies set out in the 2026 exceptions Order. It creates no new duties, makes no changes to existing processes, and imposes no new requirements on providers, families or public bodies.

The proposals for the 2026 exceptions Order were consulted upon in 2025. I'm content that no further consultation was required for this consequential amendment instrument because its changes are minor and of a technical nature. This amendment Order only updates legislative cross-references to ensure that the statute book is accurate.

I am aware that further consequential amendments are required to legislation within the competence of the United Kingdom and Scottish Governments. These are minor and technical amendments to update references to the 2010 exceptions Order to ensure consistency and accuracy. My officials are working with both Governments to support these amendments to be made prior to the 2026 exceptions Order coming into force. I therefore ask Members to approve this necessary technical Order. Thank you.

Mae hwn yn offeryn diwygio byr a thechnegol sy'n ofynnol i gadw'r llyfr statud yn glir, yn gywir ac yn gyson. Bydd Gorchymyn Eithriadau Gwarchod Plant a Gofal Dydd (Dirymu a Darpariaeth Drosiannol) (Cymru) (Diwygio) 2026 yn disodli Gorchymyn Eithriadau Gwarchod Plant a Gofal Dydd (Cymru) 2010 o 1 Ebrill 2027.

O ganlyniad i ddirymu a disodli Gorchymyn eithriadau 2010 gyda Gorchymyn eithriadau 2026, rhaid diweddaru cyfeiriadau at Orchymyn eithriadau 2010 mewn deddfwriaeth bresennol. Mae'r Gorchymyn diwygio hwn yn gwneud y newidiadau angenrheidiol hynny. Mae'r Gorchymyn diwygio hwn yn disodli cyfeiriadau perthnasol at Orchymyn eithriadau 2010 yn y llyfr statud gyda chyfeiriadau at Orchymyn eithriadau 2026.

Nid yw'r Gorchymyn diwygio hwn yn newid y polisi a nodir yng Ngorchymyn eithriadau 2026. Nid yw'n creu unrhyw ddyletswyddau newydd, nid yw'n gwneud unrhyw newidiadau i brosesau presennol, ac nid yw'n gosod unrhyw ofynion newydd ar ddarparwyr, teuluoedd na chyrff cyhoeddus.

Ymgynghorwyd ar y cynigion ar gyfer Gorchymyn eithriadau 2026 yn 2025. Rwy'n fodlon nad oedd angen ymgynghoriad pellach ar gyfer yr offeryn diwygio canlyniadol hwn oherwydd bod ei newidiadau yn fân a thechnegol. Mae'r Gorchymyn diwygio hwn yn diweddaru croesgyfeiriadau deddfwriaethol yn unig i sicrhau bod y llyfr statud yn gywir.

Rwy'n ymwybodol bod angen diwygiadau canlyniadol pellach i ddeddfwriaeth sydd o fewn cymhwysedd Llywodraethau'r Deyrnas Gyfunol a'r Alban. Mae'r rhain yn ddiwygiadau mân a thechnegol i ddiweddaru cyfeiriadau at Orchymyn eithriadau 2010 i sicrhau cysondeb a chywirdeb. Mae fy swyddogion yn gweithio gyda'r ddwy Lywodraeth i gefnogi'r diwygiadau hynny sydd i'w gwneud cyn i orchymyn eithriadau 2026 ddod i rym. Rwyf felly yn gofyn i'r Aelodau gymeradwyo'r Gorchymyn technegol angenrheidiol hwn. Diolch.

contributions.text_english:
Thank you very much, Dirprwy Lywydd. I move the motion, and I recommend that the Senedd does consent to the relevant provisions in the Armed Forces Bill 2026, as is outlined in the legislative consent motion laid for this Bill.  

The Bill introduces provisions across a broad range of areas related to the armed forces, in devolved and reserved areas alike. These include: renewing the Armed Forces Act 2006; expanding the legal duty to give due regard to the armed forces covenant to include the UK Government and the devolved Governments; to create a new defence housing service to improve standards in defence housing and their supply; improving the measures that safeguard against sexual and violent conduct, stalking and harassment; and modernising support for victims of crimes committed by the armed forces.

We believe that a number of the Bill's provisions relate to devolved services, and our legislative consent memorandum reflects this. The UK Government agrees with us that clause 2 of the armed forces covenant initiates the legislative consent memorandum process. We are also of the view that clauses related to the new defence housing service, the support of victims in the justice system with regard to the armed forces, the management of criminals, and the Reserve Forces' and Cadets' Associations may impact devolved areas. 

Members will be familiar with the armed forces covenant: the pledge that we will together, as a nation, recognise and understand that those who serve or who have served in the armed forces, and their families, including those who have faced bereavement, should be treated fairly and should not face disadvantage. Extending the legal duties of the armed forces covenant through this Bill is something that we therefore welcome as a Government, and it aligns with the commitment made in our programme for government.

Our support for services like the Veterans' NHS Wales, armed forces liaison officers, and Supporting Service Children in Education in Wales are examples of the ways that we ensure that the covenant is visible to the armed forces community. We offer practical steps, not just warm words. This duty will hold us to account, alongside other public bodies, and we welcome this.

The covenant element of the Bill will also expand the current duty to 11 additional policy areas, including childcare, social care, personal taxation and transport. This is a significant expansion of the duty's scope. I have emphasised to the UK Government that the resources, the training and the guidance must be available to all bodies subject to the duty so that it is truly embedded and to ensure that it makes a real difference to the armed forces community.

Dirprwy Lywydd, the Armed Forces Bill 2026 provides a suitable platform for ensuring that the services and policies consider the armed forces community's circumstances appropriately the length and breadth of the UK. By the same token, it offers a way to improve housing for armed forces families and improves safeguarding measures for the victims of crimes committed by the armed forces. It also provides greater safeguards against sexual and violent conduct, stalking and harassment for members of the armed forces, including those based here in Wales.

I'm grateful to the Legislation Committee and the Equality, Human Rights and Social Justice Committee, and I thank Members for their scrutiny of the Bill. I note that both committees agree with our assessment of the Bill's provisions that call for the Senedd's consent. I'm also aware that the Legislation Committee has noted that the deadline of a fortnight for laying the legislative consent memorandum was not met, and that I had not initially confirmed a recommendation for consent to be granted. We recognise the difficulties that delays in laying legislative consent memoranda can cause in terms of committee scrutiny. I also recognise the importance of laying legislative consent memoranda as soon as possible, rather than delaying them until the Welsh Government has come to a final conclusion in terms of its recommendations. I recognise the importance of providing clear recommendations for the Senedd on legislative consent memoranda as soon as possible to support effective scrutiny. I was able to inform the committees of our stance only when correspondence with the UK Government had been completed.

In terms of the changes to the scope of the covenant's duties and guidance, Members will be aware that I wrote to the UK Government in July requesting a requirement for the Welsh Ministers to give their consent, thereby ensuring stronger constitutional safeguards for the role of Welsh Ministers in relation to the covenant. I'm pleased that the committee supported my stance but am disappointed that the UK Government did not agree to this request.

I have shared my correspondence with the UK Government, in which I raised a number of matters related to the Bill, with both committees and all Members. I hope that this has answered the points raised by the Equality, Human Rights and Social Justice Committee regarding the assurances that I received from the UK Government, and I will be discussing these with the relevant UK Minister when we meet.

I'm committed that the Welsh Government will work with the other Governments of the UK to ensure that the covenant delivers for the armed forces community. This does not mean that every service across the United Kingdom is going to be provided in the same way; it means that every service recognises the needs and circumstances of the armed forces community.

As we move towards implementation, if this Bill is passed, I will ensure that the Welsh Government continues to work closely with our partners and stakeholders in Wales. This includes the armed forces expert group, the Senedd's cross-party group on the armed forces and cadets, our regional armed forces fora and the Welsh Local Government Association's armed forces network. Most important of all, we will continue to engage with the armed forces community and we'll listen to their needs and experiences as they navigate services and support in future.

Diolch yn fawr, Ddirprwy Lywydd. Dwi'n cyflwyno'r cynnig ac yn argymell bod y Senedd yn cydsynio i'r darpariaethau perthnasol ym Mil y Lluoedd Arfog 2026, fel sydd wedi'u nodi yn y cynnig cydsyniad deddfwriaethol sydd wedi'i osod ar y Bil hwn.

Mae'r Bil yn cyflwyno darpariaethau ar draws ystod eang o feysydd sy'n ymwneud â'r lluoedd arfog, mewn meysydd datganoledig a meysydd sydd wedi'u cadw'n ôl. Mae'r rhain yn cynnwys: adnewyddu Deddf y Lluoedd Arfog 2006; ehangu'r ddyletswydd gyfreithiol i roi sylw dyladwy i gyfamod y lluoedd arfog i gynnwys Llywodraeth y Deyrnas Gyfunol a'r Llywodraethau datganoledig; creu gwasanaeth tai amddiffyn newydd i wella ansawdd tai amddiffyn a'r cyflenwad ohonyn nhw; gwella'r mesurau sy’n amddiffyn rhag ymddygiad rhywiol a threisgar, stelcio ac aflonyddu; a moderneiddio cymorth i ddioddefwyr troseddau'r lluoedd arfog.

Rŷn ni'n credu bod nifer o ddarpariaethau yn y Bil yn ymwneud â gwasanaethau datganoledig, ac mae ein memorandwm cydsyniad deddfwriaethol yn adlewyrchu hynny. Mae Llywodraeth y Deyrnas Gyfunol yn cytuno â ni bod cymal 2 o gyfamod y lluoedd arfog yn sbarduno proses y memorandwm cydsyniad deddfwriaethol. Rŷn ni hefyd o'r farn y gall cymalau sy'n ymwneud â gwasanaeth tai amddiffyn newydd, cymorth i ddioddefwyr yn system cyfiawnder y lluoedd arfog, rheoli troseddwyr, a Chymdeithas Lluoedd Arfog Wrth Gefn a Chadetiaid gael effaith ar feysydd datganoledig. 

Bydd yr Aelodau'n gwybod yn iawn am gyfamod y lluoedd arfog: yr addewid y byddwn ni gyda'n gilydd, fel cenedl, yn cydnabod ac yn deall y dylai'r rhai sy'n gwasanaethu neu sydd wedi gwasanaethu yn y lluoedd arfog, a'u teuluoedd, gan gynnwys y rhai sydd wedi cael profedigaeth, gael eu trin yn deg ac na ddylent wynebu anfantais. Mae ymestyn dyletswydd gyfreithiol cyfamod y lluoedd arfog drwy'r Bil hwn yn rhywbeth rŷn ni, felly, yn ei groesawu fel Llywodraeth, ac mae'n cyd-fynd â'n hymrwymiad ni yn ein rhaglen lywodraethu.

Mae ein cefnogaeth i wasanaethau fel gwasanaeth iechyd Cymru i gyn-filwyr, swyddogion cyswllt y lluoedd arfog, a Cefnogi Plant Milwyr mewn Addysg yng Nghymru yn enghreifftiau o'r ffyrdd rŷn ni'n sicrhau bod y cyfamod yn rhywbeth gweladwy i gymuned y lluoedd arfog. Rŷn ni'n sicrhau camau ymarferol, nid dim ond geiriau. Bydd y ddyletswydd hon yn ein dal ni i gyfrif, ynghyd â chyrff cyhoeddus eraill, ac rŷn ni'n croesawu hynny.

Bydd elfen cyfamod y Bil hefyd yn ehangu'r ddyletswydd bresennol i 11 maes polisi ychwanegol, gan gynnwys gofal plant, gofal cymdeithasol, trethiant personol a thrafnidiaeth. Mae hyn yn ehangu hyd a lled y ddyletswydd yn sylweddol. Dwi wedi pwysleisio i Lywodraeth y Deyrnas Gyfunol fod rhaid i'r adnoddau, yr hyfforddiant a'r arweiniad fod ar gael i'r holl gyrff sy'n ddarostyngedig i'r ddyletswydd, er mwyn ei gwreiddio a sicrhau ei bod yn gwneud gwahaniaeth i gymuned y lluoedd arfog.

Ddirprwy Lywydd, mae Bil y Lluoedd Arfog 2026 yn rhoi llwyfan addas i wneud yn siŵr bod gwasanaethau a pholisïau yn ystyried amgylchiadau cymuned y lluoedd arfog yn briodol, a hynny ledled y Deyrnas Gyfunol. Yn yr un modd, mae'n cynnig ffordd o wella tai i deuluoedd y lluoedd arfog a gwella mesurau amddiffyn i ddioddefwyr troseddau'r lluoedd arfog. Mae hefyd yn rhoi mwy o warchodaeth rhag ymddygiad rhywiol a threisgar, stelcio ac aflonyddu ar gyfer y rhai yn y lluoedd arfog, gan gynnwys y rhai sydd wedi'u lleoli yma yng Nghymru.

Dwi'n ddiolchgar i'r Pwyllgor Deddfwriaeth a'r Pwyllgor Cydraddoldeb, Hawliau Dynol a Chyfiawnder Cymdeithasol, ac yn diolch i'r Aelodau am graffu ar y Bil. Dwi'n nodi bod y ddau bwyllgor yn cytuno â'n hasesiad o'r darpariaethau yn y Bil sy'n gofyn am gydsyniad y Senedd. Dwi hefyd yn ymwybodol bod y Pwyllgor Deddfwriaeth wedi nodi nad oedd y terfyn amser o bythefnos ar gyfer gosod y memorandwm cydsyniad deddfwriaethol wedi'i fodloni, ac nad oeddwn i wedi cadarnhau argymhelliad ar gydsyniad i ddechrau. Rŷn ni'n cydnabod yr anawsterau y mae oedi o ran gosod memoranda cydsyniad deddfwriaethol yn eu hachosi i waith craffu effeithiol pwyllgorau. Dwi'n cydnabod hefyd bwysigrwydd gosod memoranda cydsyniad deddfwriaethol cyn gynted â phosib, yn hytrach na'u gohirio nes bod Llywodraeth Cymru wedi dod i gasgliad terfynol o ran ei hargymhelliad. Dwi'n cydnabod pwysigrwydd darparu argymhellion clir i'r Senedd ar femoranda cydsyniad deddfwriaethol cyn gynted â phosib i gefnogi gwaith craffu effeithiol. Roeddwn i'n gallu hysbysu'r pwyllgorau o'n safbwynt unwaith yr oedd yr ohebiaeth â Llywodraeth y Deyrnas Gyfunol wedi digwydd.

O ran newidiadau i gwmpas dyletswydd a chanllawiau'r cyfamod, bydd yr Aelodau yn ymwybodol fy mod i wedi ysgrifennu at Lywodraeth y Deyrnas Gyfunol ym mis Gorffennaf yn gofyn am ofyniad i gael cydsyniad Gweinidogion Cymru, gan sicrhau mesurau diogelu cyfansoddiadol cryfach ar gyfer rôl Gweinidogion Cymru mewn perthynas â'r cyfamod. Dwi'n falch fod y pwyllgor wedi cefnogi fy safbwynt ond yn siomedig na wnaeth Llywodraeth y Deyrnas Gyfunol gytuno i'r cais hwnnw.

Dwi wedi rhannu fy ngohebiaeth gyda Llywodraeth y Deyrnas Gyfunol, lle codais nifer o faterion yn ymwneud â'r Bil, gyda'r ddau bwyllgor a'r holl Aelodau. Dwi'n gobeithio bod hynny wedi bodloni'r pwyntiau a godwyd gan y Pwyllgor Cydraddoldeb, Hawliau Dynol a Chyfiawnder Cymdeithasol ynglŷn â'r sicrwydd a gefais gan Lywodraeth y Deyrnas Gyfunol, a byddaf yn trafod y rhain gyda Gweinidog y Deyrnas Gyfunol pan fyddwn i'n cyfarfod.

Dwi wedi ymrwymo i Lywodraeth Cymru weithio gyda Lywodraethau eraill y Deyrnas Gyfunol i sicrhau bod y cyfamod yn cyflawni ar gyfer cymuned y lluoedd arfog. Dyw hynny ddim yn golygu bod pob gwasanaeth ledled y Deyrnas Gyfunol yn cael ei ddarparu yn yr un modd; mae'n golygu bod pob gwasanaeth yn cydnabod anghenion ac amgylchiadau cymuned y lluoedd arfog.

Wrth symud i weithredu, os caiff y Bil hwn ei basio, byddaf yn sicrhau bod Llywodraeth Cymru yn parhau i weithio'n agos gyda'n partneriaid a'n rhanddeiliaid yng Nghymru. Mae hyn yn cynnwys grŵp arbenigol y lluoedd arfog, grŵp trawsbleidiol y Senedd ar y lluoedd arfog a'r cadetiaid, ein fforymau lluoedd arfog rhanbarthol a rhwydwaith lluoedd arfog Cymdeithas Llywodraeth Leol Cymru. Yn bwysicaf oll, byddwn ni'n parhau i ymgysylltu â chymuned y lluoedd arfog ac yn gwrando ar eu hanghenion a'u profiadau wrth lywio gwasanaethau a chymorth yn y dyfodol.

contributions.text_english:
Diolch, Ddirprwy Lywydd. I'd like to begin by thanking my fellow committee members for their work on the legislative consent memorandum, which was laid before I was elected Chair. The committee has considered 15 memoranda since June 2026. It has been a significant body of work. Our report on this memorandum raises issues that are common to many of those other memoranda. I will begin by addressing those common themes.

The Welsh Government's view on whether the Senedd should grant consent to the relevant provisions in a Bill is an important part of the legislative consent process. It helps Senedd committees to come to an informed view about the legislative consent memorandum. Unfortunately, like every other memorandum laid by the Welsh Government to date, this memorandum did not include a recommendation on consent. The reason given in the memorandum was that the Welsh Government needed to analyse the wider impact of the UK legislative programme for Wales before it could come to a view. The same approach was taken across the first eight memoranda laid by this Welsh Government. We do not accept that a decision to carry out an analysis of the impact of the UK Government's legislative programme is an acceptable reason for not including a consent recommendation in a memorandum. We note the Counsel General's assurances that these eight memoranda were laid during the particular circumstances of a King's Speech coinciding with the formulation of a new Welsh Government. The Welsh Government has since agreed its principles on UK legislation in devolved areas. We hope these will now be used when the Government is determining its recommendations on consent.

We eventually received the Deputy First Minister's recommendations on consent on 24 September, four months after the Bill was reintroduced. Standing Orders state that legislative consent memoranda should normally be laid within two weeks. Not one memorandum laid by this Welsh Government to date has met that deadline. This memorandum was laid a little over five weeks after the reintroduction of the Bill. In her response to our report, which we received at 16:13 yesterday, the Deputy First Minister states that this is because the new Government needed to consider this Bill in detail. The Bill was reintroduced very shortly after the Senedd election. We accept that this is likely to have implications for the ability of the Welsh Government to adhere to the two-week deadline. However, officials working under the previous Welsh Government had already carried out a legal analysis of the Bill during the sixth Senedd, before it was subject to a carry-over motion. And, as I have noted above, there was no recommendation on consent from the Deputy First Minister. We therefore see no reason why the memorandum could not have been laid within two weeks of the reintroduction of the Bill.

I will now move on to the specific issues relating to the Bill before us today. First, on consent: we agree with the Welsh Government's assessment in the memorandum about which provisions require the Senedd's consent. Second, on delegated powers: the Welsh Government's principles on UK legislation in devolved areas state that powers to make subordinate legislation in devolved areas should be conferred on the Welsh Ministers alone. The principles also state that, where powers are conferred onto the Secretary of State and the Welsh Ministers concurrently, there should be a duty for the Secretary of State to seek the consent of the Welsh Ministers before exercising them. However, there are a number of provisions in the Bill that confer subordinate legislation-making powers in devolved areas on the Secretary of State alone.

One such power enables the Secretary of State to change which Welsh public bodies are subject to the covenant duty. The Secretary of State must consult the Welsh Ministers before exercising these powers. The Deputy First Minister requested that this be changed to a duty to obtain consent of the Welsh Ministers. The UK Government declined. The Deputy First Minister wrote that, while she favours a consent requirement, she does not anticipate circumstances where changes would be made to the duty or guidance without sufficient consultation. Can the Deputy First Minister guarantee that Welsh Ministers will be meaningfully consulted about the changes to the scope of the Bill or to the statutory guidance by this and future UK Governments? More fundamentally, the UK Government has declined to address a matter that appears to be a red line for the Welsh Government. Given this breach of the Welsh Government's principles, can the Deputy First Minister clarify why she's recommending that the Senedd gives its consent to the Bill? Diolch.

In her response to our report, which we received at 16:13 yesterday, the Deputy First Minister states that this is because the new Government needed to consider this Bill in detail. The Bill was reintroduced very shortly after the Senedd election. We accept that this is likely to have implications for the ability of the Welsh Government to adhere to the two-week deadline. However, officials working under the previous Welsh Government had already carried out a legal analysis of the Bill during the sixth Senedd, before it was subject to a carry-over motion. And, as I have noted above, there was no recommendation on consent from the Deputy First Minister. We therefore see no reason why the memorandum could not have been laid within two weeks of the reintroduction of the Bill.

I will now move on to the specific issues relating to the Bill before us today. First, on consent: we agree with the Welsh Government's assessment in the memorandum about which provisions require the Senedd's consent. Second, on delegated powers: the Welsh Government's principles on UK legislation in devolved areas state that powers to make subordinate legislation in devolved areas should be conferred on the Welsh Ministers alone. The principles also state that, where powers are conferred onto the Secretary of State and the Welsh Ministers concurrently, there should be a duty for the Secretary of State to seek the consent of the Welsh Ministers before exercising them. However, there are a number of provisions in the Bill that confer subordinate legislation-making powers in devolved areas on the Secretary of State alone.

One such power enables the Secretary of State to change which Welsh public bodies are subject to the covenant duty. The Secretary of State must consult the Welsh Ministers before exercising these powers. The Deputy First Minister requested that this be changed to a duty to obtain consent of the Welsh Ministers. The UK Government declined. The Deputy First Minister wrote that, while she favours a consent requirement, she does not anticipate circumstances where changes would be made to the duty or guidance without sufficient consultation. Can the Deputy First Minister guarantee that Welsh Ministers will be meaningfully consulted about the changes to the scope of the Bill or to the statutory guidance by this and future UK Governments? More fundamentally, the UK Government has declined to address a matter that appears to be a red line for the Welsh Government. Given this breach of the Welsh Government's principles, can the Deputy First Minister clarify why she's recommending that the Senedd gives its consent to the Bill? Diolch.

Diolch, Deputy Llywydd. As Chair of the Equality, Human Rights and Social Justice Committee, I am pleased to contribute to this debate on the legislative consent motion for the Armed Forces Bill. I am sure Members across the Chamber will recognise the significant contribution made by serving personnel, veterans and military families to communities throughout Wales. They make sacrifices on behalf of us all, and they should not face disadvantage when accessing the public services on which we all rely.

That principle sits at the heart of the armed forces covenant. It is a principle that the Senedd supported when considering the previous Armed Forces Bill in 2021, and it remains as important today as it was then. Members previously recognised that veterans, service personnel and their families should not be disadvantaged in accessing housing, healthcare and education, while also emphasising the importance of respecting devolved responsibilities in Wales. This Bill seeks to build on that foundation by extending existing covenant duties and bringing a wider range of public decision makers within scope. As the Welsh Government has noted, this would be the first time that both the UK and devolved Governments would be subject to these requirements. Our committee recognised from the outset that support for the armed forces community spans both reserved and devolved responsibilities. Defence itself is reserved, but many of the services that veterans and their families rely upon, including housing and aspects of social support, are devolved. That makes effective partnership working essential.

During our scrutiny, we sought further information from the Welsh Government on several important matters, and we thank the Deputy First Minister for engaging constructively with us in correspondence on the matters of interest to our members. First, we wanted confidence that the expanded duties would be implemented in a way that reflects Welsh circumstances. We welcome the assurances that the Welsh Government will continue to work closely with the Ministry of Defence and other Governments across the UK to improve co-ordination of support for veterans and service families. Secondly, we raised concerns about resources. New duties can create additional expectations and pressures for public bodies. At a time when budgets remain stretched, it is entirely reasonable to ask how any additional costs will be monitored and supported. We therefore welcome the Welsh Government's engagement with the UK Government on this issue, whilst noting that the absence of additional funding remains a matter that warrants continued attention.

We also examined proposals relating to the new defence housing service and the future use of Ministry of Defence land. Members will appreciate that housing is a matter of significant importance in every part of Wales. Opportunities to improve accommodation for service families are welcomed. Equally, any proposals involving defence land must be transparent, must respect Welsh planning processes, and must be developed in partnership with local communities. For that reason, we welcomed assurances that the new defence housing service will engage fully with local planning processes in Wales, and that compulsory acquisition powers would remain subject to established safeguards. We also welcome the commitment to work jointly with the Welsh Government to explore further opportunities relating to defence land and housing development.

The committee notes that differences remain between the Welsh and UK Governments regarding the extent of provisions that engage devolved competence. Nevertheless, we welcome the fact that the Welsh Government pressed UK Ministers for further information and assurances during the passage of the Bill and is now satisfied with those assurances. Therefore, while continuing to emphasise the need for ongoing scrutiny, particularly regarding funding implications and the future use of MOD land, the committee concluded that the Senedd should grant legislative consent. The committee therefore recommends that Members support today's legislative consent motion.

contributions.text_english:
Reform UK supports the Armed Forces Bill, and Reform Wales will be supporting this LCM. Reform in Wales will always be proud to support veterans here in Wales. The armed forces covenant is a commitment of real significance. It provides that those who have served should suffer no disadvantage as a consequence of their service, and that special provision is justified for those who are willing to make the ultimate sacrifice for this country. For those who are willing to give everything for this country, the covenant represents the country's duty and obligation to them in return. That obligation carries particular weight here in Wales. An estimated 115,000 veterans live here—although this number is likely to be much higher—representing 4.5 per cent of residents aged 16 and over, compared to 3.8 per cent in England.

Local health boards and NHS trusts in Wales have been subject to a statutory duty to have due regard to the covenant since November 2022. The Bill extends that duty to the Welsh Ministers themselves and broadens its scope to include health and social care, employment, transport, social security and criminal justice. However, a statutory duty is of value only when it can be relied upon, and, in healthcare, the Welsh Government has already failed to effectively implement the covenant. Welsh health circular WHC/2023/022 provides that veterans should receive priority treatment for service-related conditions over other patients with the same clinical need, yet only 15 per cent of GP practices in Wales are accredited as veteran friendly. Veterans' NHS Wales, the dedicated mental health service for veterans, who I volunteer for, does vital work but receives only £920,000 a year. That is about £8 per veteran.

The Armed Forces Bill is a welcome step forward, but it is not enough on its own. We will support the motion today because we believe in both the Armed Forces Bill and the covenant it upholds. But we will be holding the Government to account over these duties and obligations coming into effect. And we will judge this Government by the outcomes it achieves for veterans. Diolch.

contributions.text_english:
I welcome this legislative consent memorandum for the Armed Forces Bill. My son, Emyr, serves in the 1st Regiment Royal Horse Artillery, so I value the opportunity to speak on this matter today. This Bill recognises a range of items, from the issue of defence housing and property, the armed forces covenant, as well as protecting victims of service offences. These issues directly impact thousands of Welsh armed forces personnel who serve.

This LCM seeks consent on defence housing and other property, which makes provisions for a 10-year plan to build new homes across a third of the Ministry of Defence estate. I welcome this, as veteran homelessness is a serious issue not just in Wales, but across the United Kingdom as a whole. I strongly believe that armed forces personnel and veterans must be provided with clear signposting and support on issues such as housing, in order to make a transition back to civilian life when that time eventually comes.

The armed forces covenant aims to provide further support to current armed forces personnel and veterans. I would hope that my son Emyr, as well as all other military personnel, are supported and that they receive access to essential services and are treated fairly.

Robust reforms are also needed to modernise the investigation, charging and disciplining procedures for victims of service offences. A protection towards armed forces personnel is seen here, with improvements of support for protecting the victims of the most serious offences from further harm. For these reasons, I am in support of granting consent to this LCM. We owe it to our troops and our veterans. Diolch yn fawr.

contributions.text_english: Deputy First Minister, as co-chair of the cross-party group on the armed forces and cadets, I welcome this Bill and the strengthening of the armed forces covenant. Our service personnel, veterans and their families deserve our full support. But paragraph 25 of the Government's LCM makes clear that implementation costs in Wales must be met from existing budgets, with no additional UK Government funding. So, I'd like to ask you, Deputy First Minister: what assessment has your Government made of these costs, and how will you ensure that already stretched local authorities and health boards have the resources and the guidance they need to meet their expanded duties under the covenant? Diolch.

contributions.text_english: I call on the Cabinet Minister to reply to the debate.

contributions.text_english:
Diolch yn fawr, Ddirprwy Lywydd. In closing this debate, I'd like to thank both the committees and the Members for their contributions to today's debate. I think holding this debate today ensures that the Senedd's views are heard and represented in the passage of this important legislation. That passage is ongoing. The UK Government has today tabled further amendments to the Bill. So, if these amendments are deemed as requiring a further LCM, I will ensure the Senedd are updated and a supplementary LCM is laid.

I want to respond firstly to the points made by the Chair of the Legislation Committee. I absolutely recognise, and I said this in my opening remarks, the importance of providing the Senedd with clear recommendations on legislative consent memoranda at the earliest opportunity to support effective scrutiny. However, I also recognise the importance of laying legislative consent memoranda as soon as possible, rather than delaying them until the Welsh Government has reached a conclusion on its recommendation. I was able to inform the committees of the position once those discussions with the UK Government had taken place. 

As regards the requirement for the new Government to consider this Bill in detail in light of its manifesto commitments, that's why the initial two-week deadline for laying this LCM for the Bill wasn't met. We recognise the difficulties that delayed LCMs cause for effective scrutiny; nonetheless, we are committed to the effective discharge of the legislative consent process and adherence to the two-week deadline.

As regards my recommendation, the Bill makes provision about the armed forces covenant legal duty of due regard, both extending its application to the Welsh Government and extending the policy areas it applies to. We have a programme for government commitment, as I outlined, to uphold the principles of the covenant, and I think this duty will help us and other public bodies to uphold the covenant by requiring the armed forces community to be considered when key decisions on policy are taken.

I want to turn to the points made by the Chair of the human rights, equality and social justice committee—I still want to call it ESJ. On the specific points that you made, I welcome the committee's support for some of the points that I made in my correspondence to the committee. I just want to quickly touch on some of the points that you made, specifically around housing, because I think that the committee raised valid points around the DHS and the disposal of surplus defence land in Wales, which could support our house-building goals. I'm pleased that Welsh Government and MOD officials met on 14 September to discuss this issue and others relating to the DHS. I just want to give assurance that my officials have agreed to work in partnership to explore any opportunities defence land may present in terms of house building and other Government priorities, and I'll update the Senedd as soon as these discussions develop.

I'd also like to make Members aware that, on 30 November, I will be taking a paper to Cabinet regarding our approach to the armed forces covenant to co-ordinate our work across Government and drive progress in the area. We've also convened a Wales covenant conference before that, on 19 November, in Swansea, bringing together the armed forces, UK Government, public bodies and the private and third sectors to share best practice and explore the challenges we need to address collectively around the covenant, many of which have been highlighted by Members across the Siambr today.
